summary: E2E tests: run the Playwright suite in parallel
_description:
The end-to-end test suite runs every test on a single Playwright worker, so its
wall-clock time grows with each spec added. It now holds 101 tests across 24 spec
files and takes about 5 minutes. CI runs the whole suite twice, once with
`SCRIPT_DEBUG` on and once off, each under a 20-minute job timeout.

This is a good time to set up a parallel run suite that uses more Playwright workers, a set a good practices model before new specs are added.

High level plan:

 * '''Split the suite.''' The specs that make the site unusable run on their own. Everything else runs in parallel.
 * '''Isolate the test data.''' Each test creates the posts, pages, media, terms and users it needs and deletes them afterwards, instead of clearing shared data or reading unfiltered admin lists. Some specs already do this and are the model for the rest.
 * '''Use test locks for what is left.''' A few tests read a site-wide list or change a site setting, and no amount of isolation makes them safe side by side. Named locks keep only those tests apart, rather than making the whole suite serial. Playwright 1.64 supports locks and is already in place.

summary: `get_allowed_http_origins()` should not trust the insecure origin of an HTTPS site
_description:
The `get_allowed_http_origins()` function always adds both the `http://` and `https://` variants of the admin and home host to the allowed origins list, regardless of the site's scheme. On a site served only over HTTPS, the `http://` origin is therefore trusted even though the site doesn't use it.

This feeds `send_origin_headers()` which reflects a matching `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. A network attacker who can tamper with plaintext HTTP traffic can issue a credentialed cross-origin request to the HTTPS site and read the response.

Fix: Add the `http://` origin only when the corresponding `admin_url()`/`home_url()` is not HTTPS.

Related: #43428 

Originally reported by talkemade on HackerOne.

summary: WP_Filesystem_SSH2 should verify the server's host key
_description:
`WP_Filesystem_SSH2::connect()` opens the connection with `ssh2_connect()` and then authenticates, without checking the server's host key. The `hostkey` option passed to `ssh2_connect()` only sets which key algorithms are accepted. It doesn't pin a key.

The PHP manual for `ssh2_connect()` recommends checking the key with `ssh2_fingerprint()` after connecting.

Possible approaches:

- Accept an expected fingerprint, through a constant such as `FTP_HOST_FINGERPRINT` or a field in the connection form. Compare it with `ssh2_fingerprint()` before authenticating, and refuse the connection if they don't match.
- Store the fingerprint the first time the site connects and refuse later connections if it changes, like OpenSSH's `known_hosts`.

Props lboy for the original report on HackerOne.

KSES: Allow CSS color functions in inline styles
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84213.

safecss_filter_attr() drops any declaration whose value uses a CSS color function, such as rgb(), hsl(), oklch() or color-mix(). So box-shadow: 1px 1px 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.5) never reaches the page. The same goes for a shadow or text color from the style engine.

It removes a color function from the test string, innermost first, only when its contents are plain color syntax. Anything left over, such as a parenthesis, backslash, comment or unknown function, is still rejected. The check runs before the safecss_filter_attr_allow_css filter, so a plugin can still reject the declaration.

summary: Check for a non-string _method parameter in WP_REST_Server::serve_request()
_description:
`WP_REST_Server::serve_request()` lets the `_method` query parameter override the request method. It only checks that `_method` is set ( [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-server.php#L438-L439 GH] ) and then passes it to `WP_REST_Request::set_method()`, which calls `strtoupper()` on it ( [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/trunk/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php#L206 GH] ). A string like `?_method=POST` works fine, but `?_method[]=POST` makes it an array. This happens before routing, so any REST API URL can reach it. You can easily create a PHP fatal error by sending an array: {{{ $ curl -g -i 'localhost:8889/wp-json/?_method[]=POST' HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx/1.29.7 Date: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 21:14:49 GMT Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8 Transfer-Encoding: chunked Connection: keep-alive X-Powered-By: PHP/8.3.30 X-Robots-Tag: noindex Link: ; rel="https://api.w.org/" X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: strtoupper(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given in /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php:206 Stack trace: #0 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php(206): strtoupper(Array) #1 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-server.php(439): WP_REST_Request->set_method(Array) #2 /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api.php(496): WP_REST_Server->serve_request('/') #3 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp-hook.php(369): rest_api_loaded(Object(WP)) #4 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp-hook.php(393): WP_Hook->apply_filters('', Array) #5 /var/www/src/wp-includes/plugin.php(582): WP_Hook->do_action(Array) #6 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp.php(417): do_action_ref_array('parse_request', Array) #7 /var/www/src/wp-includes/class-wp.php(877): WP->parse_request('') #8 /var/www/src/wp-includes/functions.php(1375): WP->main('') #9 /var/www/src/wp-blog-header.php(16): wp() #10 /var/www/src/_index.php(17): require('/var/www/src/wp...') #11 /var/www/src/index.php(19): require_once('/var/www/src/_i...') #12 {main} thrown in /var/www/src/wp-includes/rest-api/class-wp-rest-request.php on line 206
}}} WordPress needs to check that `_method` is a string before using it to override the request method. Instead of a `HTTP 200` the response should be `400 Bad Request` with JSON data indicating it what the error is. I have a PR to address this.

summary: REST batch requests can pass WP_Error to rest_post_dispatch, causing TypeError
_description:
WordPress 7.1.3 can produce an HTTP 500 response when a REST API batch subrequest is short-circuited by a rest_pre_dispatch filter returning a WP_Error.

The REST batch handler in WP_REST_Server::serve_batch_request_v1() does not appear to normalize this error into a WP_REST_Response before invoking rest_post_dispatch.

Because rest_ensure_response() intentionally preserves WP_Error objects, callbacks expecting a REST response can receive an unexpected object type and trigger a PHP TypeError.

This appears to be a batch-processing equivalent of the issue previously addressed in #56566.

== Environment ==

* WordPress: 7.1.3
* PHP: 8.2.34 and 8.2.35
* Web server: Apache 2.4 with PHP-FPM
* Operating system: Debian 12

== Actual Behavior ==

Production logs recorded the following fatal error:

{{{
PHP Fatal error: Uncaught TypeError:
_wp_connectors_rest_settings_dispatch():
Argument #1 ($response) must be of type WP_REST_Response,
WP_Error given

wp-includes/connectors.php:697
}}}

The stack trace includes:

{{{
WP_REST_Server->serve_batch_request_v1()
WP_REST_Server->respond_to_request()
WP_REST_Server->dispatch()
}}}

The error occurred three times on October 13, 2026, and three additional times on October 25, 2026.

Each occurrence corresponded closely to an HTTP 500 response.

The issue was observed before and after upgrading PHP from 8.2.34 to 8.2.35.

== Root Cause Analysis ==

Source inspection indicates that serve_batch_request_v1() handles rest_pre_dispatch results differently from the normal REST dispatch path.

When a rest_pre_dispatch filter returns a WP_Error, the batch handler can bypass normal dispatch processing.

The batch handler subsequently executes logic equivalent to:

{{{
$result = rest_ensure_response( $result );

$result = apply_filters(
‘rest_post_dispatch’,
$result,
$this,
$single_request
);
}}}

However, rest_ensure_response() returns WP_Error objects unchanged.

Consequently, rest_post_dispatch can receive a WP_Error rather than the expected response object.

In WordPress 7.1.3, _wp_connectors_rest_settings_dispatch() requires a WP_REST_Response, producing the observed fatal error.

== Expected Behavior ==

When a REST batch subrequest returns a WP_Error through rest_pre_dispatch, WordPress should normalize that error into an appropriate REST response before invoking rest_post_dispatch.

For example, a batch subrequest producing a WP_Error with HTTP status 403 should result in:

* An outer batch response with HTTP status 207.
* A nested subrequest response with HTTP status 403.
* The original REST error code and message preserved.
* No PHP fatal error.

== Suggested Fix ==

Normalize WP_Error objects before applying rest_post_dispatch within serve_batch_request_v1().

For example:

{{{
$result = rest_ensure_response( $result );

if ( is_wp_error( $result ) ) {
$result = $this->error_to_response( $result );
}

$result = apply_filters(
‘rest_post_dispatch’,
$result,
$this,
$single_request
);
}}}

This would align the batch handler with the error normalization already implemented in the normal REST dispatch path.

The proposed correction is based on source inspection and has not yet been validated by automated tests.

== Suggested Regression Test ==

A PHPUnit test could:

1. Register a valid REST route supporting batch requests.
2. Add a rest_pre_dispatch filter returning a 403 WP_Error for that route.
3. Dispatch a request through /batch/v1.
4. Assert that the outer response returns HTTP 207.
5. Assert that the nested response returns HTTP 403 with the expected error code.
6. Verify that rest_post_dispatch receives a valid response object.

Source inspection suggests that a valid batch subrequest can trigger this condition when a rest_pre_dispatch filter returns WP_Error. This has not yet been independently verified with a regression test.

== Related Tickets ==

‘’’#56566 — Fatal error when WP_REST_Server::dispatch() returns WP_Error’’’

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/56566

This ticket corrected a similar error-normalization problem in the normal REST dispatch path. The batch handler appears to have an equivalent unhandled path.

‘’’#66136 — REST batch request handling issue’’’

https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/66136

This concerns malformed batch subrequest paths and appears distinct from the error-normalization issue described here.

== Testing Status ==

The issue has been observed repeatedly in production logs, and the relevant WordPress source code has been inspected.

A standalone PHPUnit reproduction has not yet been executed.

The identity of the rest_pre_dispatch callback responsible for producing the original WP_Error in production has not been established.

No WordPress core files were modified on the affected installation.

This report is being submitted to document the failure and proposed correction for further investigation and testing by WordPress core contributors.

summary: Abilities API: Share schema-based input coercion across execution paths
_description:
The Abilities API accepts some input values during schema validation without converting them to the types declared by the schema. For example, array properties can accept comma- or whitespace-separated strings, and object properties can accept PHP `stdClass` instances.

`WP_Ability::validate_input()` uses the REST schema validator, which normalizes a temporary copy when validating these values. Direct `WP_Ability::execute()` calls can therefore pass validation while still passing the original types to permission and execution callbacks.

The REST ability run controller already handles schema-based input coercion following #65594. Move this logic into a shared method on `WP_Ability` so direct callers and adapters receive consistent behavior without individual abilities repeating normalization.

Coercion should run after successful validation and before permission checks, ensuring permission and execution callbacks receive the same input. Coercing before validation could silently accept invalid input by removing unknown properties or casting invalid values.

Preserve the REST controller's handling of sanitization errors, respect validation filters, and review lifecycle hook ordering and compatibility with callbacks expecting original input types.

Follow-up to #66370, discussed in [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14722 PR #14722].

summary: Left/right aligned blocks have the wrong margin side in RTL
_description:
The `.alignleft` / `.alignright` layout rules combine a physical `float` with logical `margin-inline-*` margins. In RTL the 2em gap lands against the container edge instead of between the block and the wrapping text.

Switching to `margin-left` / `margin-right` fixes this. LTR output is unchanged.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Set the site language to Arabic or Hebrew.
2. Add an Image block, align it Left, and set its width to around 400px.
3. Add a long Paragraph after it.
4. On the front end, the gap is at the container edge instead of between the image and the text.

Gutenberg issue: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/40501
Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/83520

summary: REST API: Template and template part collections fetch every template again to build its links
_description:
`WP_REST_Templates_Controller::prepare_item_for_response()` passes only the template ID to `prepare_links()`. When the post type supports revisions, `prepare_links()` calls `get_block_template()` for every item, only to read `wp_id` for the revision links (added in [56819], #56922). That is another `WP_Query` per item, and for theme file templates another file read and Block Hooks pass, and the result is discarded.

Measured on 7.2-beta1 with Ipsum, as admin, `rest_do_request()`, median of 5:

|| '''Endpoint''' || '''Queries''' || '''Time''' ||
|| `/wp/v2/template-parts` (8 items) || 9 to 1 || 12.7 to 6.5 ms ||
|| `/wp/v2/templates` (11 items) || 17 to 6 || 23.3 to 17.2 ms ||

The patch hands the template that is being prepared to `prepare_links()` through a private property, so the `prepare_links( $id )` signature stays the same for subclasses, and falls back to `get_block_template()` otherwise. The response is unchanged; a test checks that the revision links are still there. PR: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14849

AI assistance: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for finding this, drafting the patch and tests, and measuring. I reviewed the patch.

summary: Secrets API: Site Health misreports the secrets backend and gives key advice that locks stored secrets
_description:
Follow-up to [64337] (#66187), found while testing 7.2-beta1.

'''1. Site Health advice that locks every stored secret.''' On a site without `WP_SECRETS_KEY`, the key source test says to "Define WP_SECRETS_KEY with a value from `wp secret generate-key`". That command is not in core or WP-CLI (the commands stayed in the feature plugin, per [64337]). Following the advice after any secret is stored makes every stored secret unreadable and blocks saving new ones, because the root key stays wrapped with the previous site key and nothing in core re-wraps it (`rotate_site_key()` has no caller). Site Health then reports the new key as good.

Reproduced on trunk:
 1. `wp_set_secret( 'test/api-key', 'value' )`, read back fine. Site Health: recommended, "Define WP_SECRETS_KEY with a value from `wp secret generate-key`".
 2. Define `WP_SECRETS_KEY` as a base64 random 32-byte value: `wp_get_secret()` returns `secret_key_unavailable`, `wp_set_secret()` fails too, and the key source test says "Secrets API is using a dedicated key" (good).
 3. Remove the constant: the secret reads back again.

This is the Site Health side of the risk @Clorith raised in #66187 comment:23 for salt rotation. It does not change the salt fallback itself.

'''2. A broken backend reads as healthy.''' The undecryptable and rotation tests turn the `WP_Error` from `wp_list_secrets()` into an empty result ("All secrets can be decrypted", "No secrets are pending rotation"). The key source test detects a broken `secrets.php` by matching "broken" in a translated string, so on translated sites it reports "using a dedicated key".

'''3. Provider drop-ins get the wrong advice.''' With a `secrets.php` that replaces the provider (a host KMS or vault), the key source test still describes the unused default keyring and recommends `WP_SECRETS_KEY`.

'''4. `secrets.php` is not listed as a drop-in.''' It loads on every request like `object-cache.php`, but `_get_dropins()` does not include it, so neither Plugins > Drop-ins nor Site Health Info shows it.

PRs: https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14847 (1 to 3, one commit each) and https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14848 (4).

AI assistance: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) for finding these, drafting the patches and tests, and running them. I reviewed the patches and reproduced the steps above on 7.2-beta1.

summary: Classic Editor: Switching from Text to Visual mode restructures HTML lists based on cursor position
_description:
Since updating to WordPress 7.1.3, I've encountered a reproducible issue with bulleted lists in the Classic Editor. Simply placing the cursor at the end of a list item in Text mode, without making any changes to the HTML, causes WordPress to restructure the list when switching back to Visual mode. All list items preceding the cursor position become nested inside an additional
    , wrapped in a new
  • element. This results in unwanted indentation and changes to otherwise valid HTML. **Steps to reproduce** 1 Create a new post using Classic Editor. 2 In Visual mode, create a bulleted list containing five items: A, B, C, D and E. 3 Switch to Text mode. 4 Place the cursor at the end of the
  • D
    • line without typing or modifying anything. 5 Switch back to Visual mode. **Actual result:** Items A, B and C become indented as a nested list. The editor inserts an additional parent list item with style="list-style-type: none;" and separates the remaining items into another list. **Expected result:** The HTML and visual formatting should remain unchanged because no edits were made. **Additional observations** The point where the list splits follows the cursor position. Switching between Text and Visual modes without repositioning the cursor does not cause the problem. The issue is reproducible in both Chrome and Microsoft Edge. The original HTML is valid. The issue appeared following recent PHP and WordPress updates. **Environment** WordPress: 7.1.3 Classic Editor plugin: 1.7.0 PHP: 8.3.36 Hosting: DreamHost Theme: Genesis child theme Browsers tested: Chrome and Microsoft Edge **Related ticket** This behaviour appears similar to WordPress Core Trac ticket #29643, which documents unwanted nested lists and insertion of
  • when switching between editing modes. https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/29643 **Attachments** Three screenshots demonstrating the original list, the resulting indentation in Visual mode, and the modified HTML in Text mode.

summary: Enqueue the classic theme styles synced from Gutenberg instead of `classic-themes.css`
_description:
`wp-includes/css/classic-themes.css` is needed to provide the default styles of some core blocks, such as the Button block, in classic themes without a `theme.json`.

Gutenberg has the same styles in [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/blob/trunk/packages/block-library/src/classic.scss classic.scss], and its build output is already synced to core as `wp-includes/css/dist/block-library/classic.css`, but this file is never loaded. Instead, core enqueues its own copy, which is outdated compared to Gutenberg and is missing the styles for the Tabs and Accordion blocks ([https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/73608 GB 73608]), [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77607 GB 77607]).

== Proposed changes

Remove the file bundled in core, and enqueue the stylesheet synced from Gutenberg as `classic-theme-styles` instead. This way, future changes to the styles will reach core through the regular package sync.

summary: Media endpoint returns 500 when an upload is rejected for a client reason
_description:
When `wp_handle_upload()` or `wp_handle_sideload()` rejects a file, `WP_REST_Attachments_Controller` returns status 500 whatever the reason:

 * `upload_from_file()`: `rest_upload_unknown_error`, 500
 * `upload_from_data()`: `rest_upload_sideload_error`, 500

Most of these rejections are caused by the request, not the server:

 * a file type the site does not allow,
 * an empty or partial file,
 * a file over `upload_max_filesize`,
 * a file a plugin rejected in `wp_handle_upload_prefilter` (size, dimension and naming policy plugins do this).

Other request checks in the same controller already return 400 (`rest_upload_no_data`, the multisite checks in `check_upload_size()`). The URL sideload path added in 7.2 also returns 400 for a disallowed type, by comparing the translated message string.

'''Why this matters more in 7.2:''' since [64588], uploads from the Media Library grid, Add New Media File and the media modal go through `POST /wp/v2/media` instead of `async-upload.php`. So every upload a plugin refuses, and every disallowed type, now shows up as an HTTP 500:

 * in server access logs,
 * in APM and uptime error rates,
 * in the browser console ("Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 500").

On 7.1 the same refusal from `async-upload.php` was a 200 with an error message.

=== Steps to reproduce (7.2-beta1-64675) ===

 1. Add this mu-plugin:
{{{#!php
<?php
add_filter( 'wp_handle_upload_prefilter', function ( $file ) {
	if ( false !== strpos( $file['name'], 'reject' ) ) {
		$file['error'] = 'Rejected by a plugin.';
	}
	return $file;
} );
}}}
 2. Go to Media > Add New Media File and upload `reject-me.jpg`. The UI shows "Rejected by a plugin.", but the request returns 500.

The same with an application password and curl:

||= Upload =||= Before =||= After =||
|| valid JPEG || 201 || 201 ||
|| `reject-me.jpg` (prefilter), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `vector.svg` (type not allowed), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `shell.php` (type not allowed), multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| empty file, multipart || 500 || 400 ||
|| `reject-me.jpg`, raw body (sideload) || 500 || 400 ||
|| `vector.svg`, raw body (sideload) || 500 || 400 ||

Error codes and messages stay the same; only the status changes.

=== Patch ===

The controller cannot tell the reasons apart today: every failure reaches it as `array( 'error' => $message )`. The patch:

 1. `_wp_handle_upload()` passes an error code as a third argument to the upload error handler. The default `wp_handle_upload_error()` returns it as `error_code`. The codes:
   * `upload_prefilter_error`
   * `upload_invalid_form`
   * `upload_err_ini_size`, `upload_err_form_size`, `upload_err_partial`, `upload_err_no_file`, `upload_err_no_tmp_dir`, `upload_err_cant_write`, `upload_err_extension`, `upload_php_error`
   * `upload_failed_test`
   * `upload_empty_file`
   * `upload_invalid_file_type`
   * `upload_dir_error`
   * `upload_move_failed`
 2. A new `WP_REST_Attachments_Controller::get_upload_error_status()` returns 400 for the client errors and 500 for everything else, including no tmp dir, can't write, an uploads directory that can't be created, a file that can't be moved, and any error without a code.
 3. The URL sideload path checks `upload_invalid_file_type` instead of comparing the translated message.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * The `error` key and every REST error code are unchanged. `error_code` is a new, optional key.
 * A custom `upload_error_handler` now receives a third argument. Userland functions ignore extra arguments. Only an internal PHP function used as the handler with a fixed argument count would complain, which seems unlikely.
 * A plugin that defines its own `wp_handle_upload_error()` before core does returns no `error_code`, so its errors keep the 500 status. Nothing changes for it.
 * Clients that treat 5xx as "retry" will no longer retry rejected uploads, which is the point. The media upload queue in `@wordpress/upload-media` decides retries from the error message, not the status, so it is unaffected. The Media Library chooses its text from the error code and message, so the UI is unchanged.

=== Open questions ===

 * Should the size errors (`upload_err_ini_size`, `upload_err_form_size`) be 413 instead of 400?
 * Should the type error use `rest_upload_invalid_file_type` everywhere, like the URL sideload path? I left the codes alone to keep the change small.

=== Tests ===

 * REST: a prefilter rejection, a disallowed type and a raw-body prefilter rejection return 400. An uploads directory that can't be created and a destination that can't be written return 500.
 * `wp_handle_sideload()` returns the right `error_code` for prefilter, empty file, type, uploads dir and move failures.
 * Eight of the ten new tests fail without the change. The two 500 tests guard the existing behavior.
 * `WP_Test_REST_Attachments_Controller`, `Tests_Admin_IncludesFile`, `Tests_Media` and `Tests_File`: 966 tests pass. The 20 warnings come from `Tests_Filesystem_WpOpcacheInvalidateDirectory` and are the same on trunk.
 * phpcs and PHPStan are clean on the changed files.

Use of AI tools: I used Claude Code to write the patch and tests, and draft this ticket. I reviewed the code and ran the tests and the reproduction myself.

Abilities API: explore allowing an ability to belong to multiple categories
_description:
Tracking ticket from the #core-ai chat: explore support for multiple categories per ability.

== Current behaviour ==

An ability must declare exactly one category, and it is required:

{{{#!php
// wp-includes/abilities-api/class-wp-ability.php
if ( empty( $args['category'] ) || ! is_string( $args['category'] ) ) {
	// "The ability properties must contain a `category` string."
}
}}}

That single slug then flows through the whole API surface:

 * `WP_Ability::get_category(): string` returns one slug.
 * `WP_Abilities_Registry::register()` rejects an ability whose category is not already registered.
 * `wp_get_abilities( array( 'category' => 'content' ) )` keeps an ability only when `$ability->get_category() === $category` — an exact, single match.
 * REST: `wp-abilities/v1/abilities` exposes `category` as a `string` response field and accepts a single-string `category` collection parameter (sanitised with `sanitize_key`); `wp-abilities/v1/categories` links each category to `…/abilities?category=<slug>`.

== Why this is limiting ==

Plenty of abilities genuinely sit in more than one bucket — generating alt text for an attachment is both "media" and "content"; exporting users to CSV is both "users" and "data export". Today the registrant has to pick one, and the fact that it also belongs elsewhere is simply lost.

Because the category is the only first-class grouping dimension, every consumer that groups or filters abilities inherits that lossiness: the Abilities Explorer, MCP tool grouping in the MCP Adapter, command-palette-style UIs. Discovery degrades — the ability is invisible under a category a user would reasonably browse. Consumers route around it with naming conventions or private `meta`, which fragments across plugins instead of being solved once in core.

== Questions to settle ==

1. **Shape.** Widen `category` to accept `string|string[]`, or add a separate plural argument (e.g. `categories`) while `category` stays the single canonical/primary one? The latter keeps a stable "which one do I display" answer for UIs and preserves back-compat for everything reading `get_category()`.
2. **Back-compat.** `get_category(): string` has a scalar return type and cannot change. Add `get_categories(): array` alongside it, with `get_category()` continuing to return the primary?
3. **Filtering semantics.** `wp_get_abilities( array( 'category' => 'x' ) )` should presumably match when `x` is any of the ability's categories. Should it also accept a list, and if so is that OR or AND?
4. **REST.** Add a `categories` array field to the abilities schema (keeping `category` for back-compat), and decide whether the `category` collection parameter accepts multiple slugs — it is string-only today.
5. **Still required?** Keep "at least one category" mandatory so discovery stays guaranteed, rather than allowing an empty list.
6. **Downstream.** Impact on the MCP Adapter's grouping and on the Abilities Explorer UI.
7. **Right model?** Is a flat multi-category list the correct answer, or is the real request tags/taxonomy alongside a single primary category?

== Related ==

 * #64345 — ability names should support versioning
 * #64209 — allow abilities to be deprecated

Both touch the same registration-shape surface.

summary: Call update_post_author_caches in wp_ajax_query_attachments function
_description:
`wp_ajax_query_attachments()` passes each attachment to `wp_prepare_attachment_for_js()`, which runs `new WP_User( $attachment->post_author )` to get the author name. The author caches are never primed, so every distinct author costs two database queries (`wp_users` and `wp_usermeta`) on each media modal request.

`WP_Query::the_post()` primes author caches in #55716, but this endpoint maps over `$attachments_query->posts` directly and never calls `the_post()`.


The same pattern is already used in `WP_Posts_List_Table` (#56100) and `wp_prepare_revisions_for_js()` (#56978).

== Results ==

Queries made by `wp_ajax_query_attachments()` before and after `update_post_author_caches`:

||= Authors =||= Attachments =||= Queries Before =||= Queries After =||
|| 10 || 40 || 26 || 8 ||
|| 50 || 100 || 106 || 8 ||

Before the change, the count grows by two queries per distinct author.

summary: Mobile Admin Menu overlaps main content and #wpfooter text when open
_description:
**Environment**
WordPress Version: 7.2-beta1
Device / OS: iOS / Safari Mobile

**Issue Description**
When viewing the WordPress Admin dashboard on a mobile screen with the sidebar navigation menu expanded (`.wp-responsive-open`), the dark left sidebar (`#adminmenuwrap`) overlays directly on top of the main content area (`#wpcontent`) and footer (`#wpfooter`). 

**Specifically:**
1. Footer Text Truncation: The left side of the admin footer text (`#wpfooter`) is covered and cut off by the dark sidebar background rather than shifting horizontally or being hidden.
2. Layout Overlap: The stacking context (`z-index`) and responsive positioning cause the sidebar to obscure the content layer instead of pushing the content container or displaying a clean full-screen backdrop.

**Steps to Reproduce**
1. Log into the WordPress Admin area on a mobile browser
2. Tap the hamburger icon (`≡`) in the top admin bar to open the responsive side menu.
3. Scroll down to the bottom of the page (e.g., Comments or Dashboard page).
4. Observe the left alignment of the footer text under the dark menu background.

Expected Behavior
When the responsive mobile menu opens, `#wpfooter` and main content should either be offset (`padding-left` / `margin-left`), covered by a unified backdrop overlay, or hidden to prevent partially readable, truncated text.

summary: render_block_core_template_part / get_404_template is called when in any admin area
_description:
it seems that no matter where you are in the admin area, render_block_core_template_part is invoked. I have no idea why this would be required when in the reading settings area, for example.

to replicate:
1. add error log to render_block_core_template_part like so:

{{{#!php

<?php
/**
 * Server-side rendering of the `core/template-part` block.
 *
 * @package WordPress
 */

/**
 * Renders the `core/template-part` block on the server.
 *
 * @since 5.9.0
 *
 * @global WP_Embed $wp_embed WordPress Embed object.
 *
 * @param array $attributes The block attributes.
 *
 * @return string The render.
 */
function render_block_core_template_part( $attributes ) {
	static $seen_ids = array();

	error_log('WHY IS THIS RENDERING ' . print_r($attributes, true));
	$template_part_id = null;
	$content          = null;
...
}}}

2. check error log, observe that header and footer template parts are there.

This is on the 2025 theme, with no other plugins installed.

Digging deeper:
It appears that in template-loader.php, when on any admin area, get_404_template is invoked... because is_404 is true, because the main query sees {{{$query_vars['p']}}} is empty, because we're not viewing a post.

So a bit more involved than I originally thought.

UPDATE: this was due to the site i was working on missing the file for the site favicon. in fetching the missing favicon, it was rendering the 404 template somewhere else. 

it's still rendering though, and it appears to be a browser plugin request. Using React Developer Tools extension attempts to look for /wp-admin/installHook.js.map, which doesn't exist, triggering the rendering of the 404 page template.

background: a block i'm working on does some complicated stuff, so I was looking to implement a simple caching / transient system to store the rendered output. This entails having a way to flush the cache - but while I was testing it in a custom admin area, there was one block transient that just wouldn't go away. as it turns out, that block was in the header template, and because of my missing favicon image, was getting invoked every time the admin area loaded, and then re-caching the block as it rendered a 404 for the favicon request. neat!

tldr: feels like 404 page templates shouldn't be rendered for requests like these, seems like a lot of extra stuff going on that doesn't need to be.

Script Loader: Add an API for stylesheet LINK tags
_description:
Stylesheet `<link>` tags in WordPress Core are largely built as HTML strings, so adding attributes such as a CSP `nonce`, `integrity`, or `crossorigin` often requires modifying markup through `style_loader_tag`. Scripts already have `wp_get_script_tag()` and the `wp_script_attributes` filter, while #51325 proposes the corresponding API for inline `<style>` tags.

The proposed API introduces `wp_get_style_link_tag()`, `wp_print_style_link_tag()`, and the `wp_style_attributes` filter, using `WP_HTML_Tag_Processor` to validate and escape attributes.

The implementation is split into three PRs:

* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14498 PR #14498]: Adds the API and uses it in `WP_Styles::do_item()`, including right-to-left and alternate stylesheets, `wp_admin_css()`, and `locale_stylesheet()`.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14499 PR #14499]: Updates the remaining Core call sites in `wp_ajax_parse_embed()`, `wp_ajax_parse_media_shortcode()`, and the deprecated theme compatibility header.
* [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14500 PR #14500]: Updates Twenty Ten and Twenty Eleven, with a fallback for older WordPress versions.

PRs #14499 and #14500 depend on #14498.

== Backward compatibility ==

The existing `style_loader_tag` and `wp_admin_css` filters remain available. Unlike the changes to script tags in [56687], the historical quoting, escaping, and attribute order are preserved for existing attributes that `wp_style_attributes` does not modify. The new attributes filter runs before the legacy filters.

The filter cannot change or remove an existing `id`, since other code may depend on it. `style_loader_tag` also continues to receive the original escaped URL, even if `wp_style_attributes` modifies `href`.

One compatibility change is that `WP_Styles::do_item()` now uses `get_src()` instead of `_css_href()`, so subclasses overriding `_css_href()` no longer affect the printed URL.

Additionally, stylesheet URLs previously printed without escaping by `locale_stylesheet()` and the remaining Core call sites in PR #14499 are now escaped.

wp_insert_user() allows duplicate email addresses containing an apostrophe
_description:
== Description ==

`wp_insert_user()` runs `pre_user_email`, which includes `wp_filter_kses`. That filter expects slashed input and returns slashed output, so for `o'brien@example.com` the value of `$user_email` at the duplicate check is `o\'brien@example.com`.

`email_exists( $user_email )` then queries for the literal backslashed string, never matches the stored row, and the duplicate check silently passes. The value is unslashed later via `wp_unslash( $compacted )`, so the duplicate is saved with the correct address.

[57711] (#52529) fixed the related comparison on update by slashing `$old_user_data->user_email`, but the `email_exists()` lookup was not changed.

== Steps to reproduce ==

Tested on trunk 7.2-alpha-63166, MariaDB 10.11.

{{{
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'a', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
wp_insert_user( wp_slash( array( 'user_login' => 'b', 'user_pass' => 'x', 'user_email' => "o'brien@example.com" ) ) );
// Second call succeeds. With plain@example.com it correctly returns existing_user_email.
}}}

Results with an existing user at `o'brien@example.com`:

||= Path =||= Result =||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, slashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_insert_user()`, unslashed input || duplicate created ||
|| `wp_update_user()` moving another user to that email || allowed ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users` (admin) || 201, duplicate created ||
|| `register_new_user()` || blocked (own `email_exists()` check) ||
|| `POST /wp/v2/users/me` (subscriber) || blocked (`rest_user_invalid_email`) ||

Front-end registration and self-service profile edits are protected by their own checks, so this needs `create_users` or direct API use. It is a data integrity issue, not a privilege escalation.

== Impact ==

Once duplicates exist, `get_user_by( 'email' )` returns whichever row the database hands back first. Anything keyed on email (password reset by email, login with email, plugins that look users up by email) can then resolve to the wrong account.

== Proposed fix ==

Run the comparison and lookup against the unslashed value, for example `$check_email = wp_unslash( $user_email );` used in both `strcasecmp()` and `email_exists()`. This could also make the slashing of `$old_user_data->user_email` from [57711] unnecessary, which is worth confirming in review.

Tests should cover insert (slashed and unslashed), update to another user's apostrophe email, and REST create, alongside the existing `test_reset_password_with_apostrophe_in_email()`.

Twenty Fourteen: Lato font lacks letters for Turkish and other Latin-script languages (requires update)
_description:
Twenty Fourteen has its own copy of the Lato font in `fonts/lato/`. The file `fonts/font-lato.css` loads these font files. The font files are Lato version 1.104 "Western+Polish". These files do not have many letters of Latin-script languages.

== Problem 1: Text shows letters from two fonts ==

When a letter is not in Lato, the browser uses a different font for that letter. The letter then looks heavier, or it has a different shape. Refer to demo.png.

This occurs on sites in these languages. Their translations keep the Lato font on, but Lato 1.104 does not have all their letters:

||= Locale =||= Letters that Lato 1.104 does not have =||
|| sk_SK || `č ď ĺ ľ ň ŕ ť` (and capitals) ||
|| hr || `č đ` (and capitals) ||
|| ro_RO || `ă ș ț` (and capitals) ||
|| hu_HU || `ő ű` (and capitals) ||
|| lv || `ā č ē ģ ī ķ ļ ņ ū` (and capitals) ||
|| lt_LT || `č ė į ų ū` (and capitals) ||
|| vi || `ă đ ơ ư` and the tone marks ||

This also occurs on sites in any language that show names or text in these languages.

== Problem 2: Some languages do not get the theme font ==

The theme has a translatable switch: `_x( 'on', 'Lato font: on or off', 'twentyfourteen' )`. Because of the missing letters, these translations set the switch to `off`:

||= Locale =||= Letters that Lato 1.104 does not have =||
|| tr_TR || `ğ ş İ` (and capitals) ||
|| az || `ə ğ ş İ` (and capitals) ||
|| cs_CZ || `č ď ě ň ř ť ů` (and capitals) ||
|| sl_SI || `č` (and capital) ||
|| bs_BA || `č đ` (and capitals) ||
|| eo || `ĉ ĝ ĥ ĵ ŝ ŭ` (and capitals) ||

Sites in these languages do not load a webfont. The CSS stays `font-family: Lato, sans-serif`, thus each visitor sees a different font:
 * Most visitors see the system font, not Lato. Thus, the design of the theme in these languages is different from the design in other languages.
 * Visitors that have a Lato font on their computer see that font. The result depends on the installed version. On my site (tr_TR), the post titles (weight 300) were very thin. Refer to site-no-webfont.png and site-lato2-webfont.png.

== Proposed fix ==

 1. Replace the font files with Lato version 2.x (latofonts.com, SIL OFL 1.1). Lato 2.015 has all the letters in the two tables above.
 2. Keep the same font family name, font weights (300, 400 and 700, normal and italic, and 900) and file names.
 3. After the update, the translation teams can change the switch back to `on`.

== Evidence ==

 * demo.png: Turkish text in Lato 1.104 (as the theme loads it) and in Lato 2.015.
 * site-no-webfont.png: a post title on a tr_TR site, without a webfont.
 * site-lato2-webfont.png: the same post title with Lato 2.015 as a webfont.
 * The switch values come from the current Twenty Fourteen language packs (api.wordpress.org/translations/themes/1.0/?slug=twentyfourteen).

Related tickets: #29690 (latin-ext subset for Polish), #55985 (self-hosted fonts), #63964 (example of an update to a bundled font).

summary: A request for a Story Editor or Plain Text Editor to make editing invisible text quicker than going to Code Viewer
_description:
I added some custom skip links to bypass some repeated blocks on the website I made, in the process of adding the skip-link classes to a URL, it makes them invisible within the WordPress editor (as they should, since they should only be visible on focus). 
{{{
skip-link screen-reader-text
}}}
The only way to check the text content of that link currently is to use the Link options in the pop-up Editor or go to the Code Editor, which will not necessarily jump to where you are, but you can Ctrl+F those classes to get to where it is. However, not everyone wants to use the Code Editor (I imagine some non-developers might find it intimidating or unnecessarily cluttered). It made me think there could be another way to do this, particularly for invisible text that isn't a link.
What I'm wondering is if there could be a way to integrate into the WordPress Editor a "Plain text preview" mode, where the editor gives the option of previewing as plain text (CSS styles removed), which would also allow any invisible text to become visible again and let you modify the text content as plain text, which would then update in the Editor. 
In InDesign and Scribus there is something like this called a "Story Editor". Those are in a publishing context rather than a website editing context, but I think the idea could have some utility here.
I'm not sure if this would need to be integrated as an entirely new preview mode like "Visual Mode", "Code Viewer", "Story Mode" or "Plain Text Mode", or if it is better to be on a per-block basis, as a "Plain text preview" option on the mini block pop-up editor that appears when you select a block in the WordPress editor (sorry I don't know what this menu is called), or as a Text Content field in the Block Sidebar. If it's a large paragraph that would need editing, a pop up menu might have issues with staying open and editable, so maybe the sidebar or a totally new preview mode would be better.
Just wanted to raise this idea in case other people have thought the same thing. It might be more convenient for quick small edits of skip links or other kinds of styles. At a minimum, you should be able to preview the text in a separate plain text window (to avoid accessibility issues with style conflicts), and modify the text.
**Some resources:** 
[https://helpx.adobe.com/indesign/desktop/add-and-manage-text/add-and-manage-text-frames/open-and-use-story-editor.html Open and use Story Editor (Adobe InDesign)]
[https://wiki.scribus.net/canvas/Working_with_Story_Editor Working with Story Editor]
Note: I realize the first version of this post neglected to mention the Link editor which does have a Plain text type field, but what I'm referring to overall is the ability to view in the editor the text through a separate mode, which could also apply to other blocks like paragraph blocks.

summary: MCP setup on the Connectors screen
_description:
== Problem ==

Settings → Connectors is WordPress's central place for setting up integrations and even promotes AI experiments and third-party proprietary AI connectors (with no inherent functionality). 

The official MCP Adapter is now available in the WordPress.org plugin directory, but a site owner who wants to connect an MCP client still has to discover the adapter, find the correct endpoint for their site, create an Application Password, and translate those details into a client-specific configuration. Activating the plugin does not currently provide that path on the Connectors screen.

This is a different task from choosing which WordPress abilities are exposed over MCP. The proposed card helps a person connect a client to their own site; exposure controls can remain with the adapter or another dedicated interface.

== Proposal ==

Add a first-party "WordPress MCP" card to Settings → Connectors. The card would guide an authorized user through:

 1. Installing and activating the official MCP Adapter (`mcp-adapter`) from the WordPress.org plugin directory through an explicit "Install and activate" action when it is missing, or an "Activate" action when it is installed but inactive. Use Core's existing Plugins REST API and normal installation and activation permissions. Show a useful explanation when installation is unavailable (for example, file modifications are disabled).
 2. Showing the site's actual MCP endpoint and whether Application Passwords are available for the current user. Resolve the endpoint from the active adapter/server registration so subdirectory installs and plain permalinks work.
 3. Choosing an MCP client and creating a separately named, revocable Application Password for that client through WordPress's existing API, only after the user requests it. Provide a copyable configuration for supported clients and a link to revoke the credential from the user's profile. (This part is debatable, perhaps it's just a link to the plugin documentation which can be updated more frequently.)
 4. Explaining what to do next, including a first test to run in the selected client and the "connected but no abilities available" state. Link to the adapter's documentation or diagnostics where appropriate.

The card should use the existing Connectors UI and WordPress design-system components. It should distinguish "adapter installed" and "ready to connect" from a verified client connection; merely showing an endpoint is not proof that a client has connected.

Application Passwords inherit the permissions of the WordPress account that creates them. The setup flow should make that clear, show the generated secret only at creation, and avoid storing it in connector settings or exposing it in subsequent page loads. If Application Passwords are unavailable, the card should explain the reason where WordPress can determine it and provide an actionable next step.

== Why in Core? ==

Core owns the Connectors screen and already provides a path for discovering and installing connector plugins. A guide supplied only by MCP Adapter or AI Experiments cannot appear before the plugin is installed, which leaves the first step undiscoverable. A first-party MCP card would make the site-to-client setup available in the same place before and after installation. The MCP server would still come from the optional MCP Adapter plugin; this proposal does not add an MCP server to Core. It also allows plugins to remove their own custom MCP setup instructions and settings pages and centralize on one UI entry point.

The working prototype below demonstrates the flow on the Connectors screen. It registers a non-credential connector and adds a custom card, but relies on experimental @wordpress/connectors JavaScript exports. Core can use the prototype to test the interaction while settling the final ownership of client configuration templates and adapter status data.

Prototype: https://github.com/bacoords/mcp-connection-guide
Live WordPress Playground demo: https://playground.wordpress.net/?blueprint-url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fbacoords%2Fmcp-connection-guide%2Fmain%2Fblueprint.json
Screenshots: https://github.com/bacoords/mcp-connection-guide/tree/main/docs/screenshots

== Suggested acceptance criteria ==

 * The card is discoverable on Settings → Connectors and can install/activate the official MCP Adapter from the plugin directory when the user has the required capabilities. No plugin installation occurs merely from viewing the page.
 * Missing adapter, inactive adapter, failed installation, disabled file modifications, unavailable Application Passwords, and insufficient permissions each have a clear state and next step.
 * The endpoint is derived from the registered MCP server and works for subdirectory installs and plain permalinks.
 * Creating a credential requires an explicit action. A separate Application Password can be named for each client; its value is shown once, is not saved in Connector settings, and has a clear revocation path.
 * Generated setup instructions use the active site's endpoint and supported authentication method. They are accessible, keyboard-operable, localizable, and built with existing WordPress UI components.
 * A site with no abilities exposed over MCP has an understandable explanation rather than appearing silently broken.

== Related work ==

 * Connectors custom-card extensibility: #64791
 * MCP Adapter in the plugin directory: https://wordpress.org/plugins/mcp-adapter/
 * MCP Adapter site-owner onboarding discussion: https://github.com/WordPress/mcp-adapter/issues/369
 * MCP Adapter Site Health diagnostics proposal: https://github.com/WordPress/mcp-adapter/pull/376
 * AI plugin MCP Access proposal, focused on ability exposure: https://github.com/WordPress/ai/pull/992
 * Earlier AI plugin MCP admin UI and client-configuration exploration (closed without merging): https://github.com/WordPress/ai/pull/152

kses filter silently strips allowfullscreen from Vimeo and YouTube iframe embeds on every post save, breaking video playback sitewide
_description:
Every time a WordPress post containing a Vimeo or YouTube iframe embed is saved or updated, the kses filter silently strips the allowfullscreen attribute from the embed code in the database. This causes the embedded video to display a privacy/playback error to all visitors with no warning to the site owner — without my knowledge. I never know how long videos have not been working. This is not acceptable.

Steps to reproduce:

Embed a Vimeo or YouTube video in a post using the standard iframe embed code provided by those platforms
Save the post
Visit the post as a visitor — the video displays: “Because of its privacy settings, this video cannot be played here”
Inspect the post content in the database — allowfullscreen has been silently removed

Why this is a defect:

WordPress’s own embed block and oEmbed system generate iframe code that includes allowfullscreen. The kses filter then strips it on save — meaning WordPress is actively breaking its own output with zero warning to the user.

allowfullscreen is not a security risk. It is a standard HTML5 attribute that permits an iframe to enter fullscreen mode. It poses no cross-site scripting risk, no injection vector, and no security concern of any kind. It has been a standard part of the HTML5 specification since 2012.

Real-world impact:

I have operated a professional WordPress broadcast platform since 2009. Over nearly two decades, I have hosted leaders from every major industry — producing close to 300 episodes of long-form video interviews and 300 audio episodes that serve as a permanent public archive. This is serious, professional publishing work on WordPress.

This issue has been silently breaking professional video publishers like me for over a decade. A site with hundreds of video episodes can have every single video broken simultaneously simply because the site owner edited and saved a post for any reason — fixing a typo, updating metadata, adding a transcript. There is no warning. Visitors see broken videos. The site owner has no idea until a visitor reports it.

I want to be more active on my site — updating content, adding transcripts for accessibility and SEO, improving posts. But every time I save a post, my entire video library breaks. This is not a theoretical edge case. This is a recurring, documented failure that is actively discouraging professional publishers from maintaining and improving their WordPress sites.

My site is itsrainmakingtime.ch — a broadcast platform that has been live on WordPress since 2009.

Requested fix:

Add allowfullscreen to the kses allowed attributes whitelist for iframe elements. This is a one-line fix that would permanently resolve a user-hostile bug that has persisted since 2012.

I respectfully urge the WordPress core team to prioritize this fix. Professional publishers deserve better.

Thank you in advance. 

Kim Greenhouse

summary: Fix duplicate <h1> landmark tags on login and password recovery pages
_description:
An accessibility (a11y) and markup validation issue exists on the core login, forgot password, and registration screens (`wp-login.php`). The page currently generates two separate `<h1>` heading landmarks simultaneously, which violates semantical HTML standards and disrupts document structure for screen reader users.

=== Root Cause Analysis
In `src/wp-login.php`, an `<h1>` tag with the class `.screen-reader-text` is dynamically outputted to act as an accessible text heading representing the active page title (e.g., "Log In"). However, directly below that landmark block, the presentation layout wraps the visible WordPress website branding logo image anchor (`.wp-login-logo`) within a second, nested `<h1>` element. 

=== Proposed Fix
The brand presentation element does not require header hierarchical value. This patch replaces the outer wrapper around the logo anchor link from an `<h1>` element to a fallback semantic block `<div>` tag with `role="presentation"`. 

This safely reduces the heading layer footprint back to a clean, single `<h1>` per view, allowing screen readers to seamlessly announce the actual utility context of the page title without configuration conflicts.

=== Environment Details
- **Affected File:** `src/wp-login.php`
- **Testing Setup:** Local WP (Flywheel dev stack)
- **Repository Branch Target:** trunk / core develop clone
https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14292

summary: Update counts in the folded admin menu don't refresh after updating a plugin
_description:

The admin menu prints each top-level item's update count twice: once in the menu link, and once in the submenu header (`.wp-submenu-head`). The submenu header is what shows when the menu is folded, either after clicking "Collapse Menu" or automatically on screens between 783 and 960 pixels wide. `wp.updates.refreshCount()` only updates the copy in the menu link, so the folded menu never changes.

=== Steps to reproduce

2. Make the browser window about 900 pixels wide, or click "Collapse Menu".
3. Go to "Plugins > Installed Plugins" and click "update now" for one of them.
4. Hover over "Plugins" in the admin menu.

Expected: the count shows 1.

Actual: it still shows 2. After updating both plugins it still shows 2 instead of no count.

The same thing happens with the "Themes" count in the network admin, which is also a top-level menu item. On a single site the theme count is on the "Themes" submenu item, so it isn't affected.

=== Environment
- WordPress: 7.2-alpha (trunk)
- Browser: Chromium 149
- Single site and multisite

I have a patch ready and will link the PR here.

summary: Site Icon in Settings > General: exact 512×512 image skips the crop step, so site icon sizes (32/180/192/270) are never generated
_description:
When a Site Icon is set from '''Settings > General''' using an image that is exactly 512×512, the media frame skips the crop step and saves the original attachment as `site_icon`. The crop step is what generates the site icon sizes (`site_icon-32`, `-180`, `-192`, `-270`), so they are never created.

`wp_site_icon()` then falls back to the closest registered size for every favicon tag, and browsers download a larger image than needed (e.g. a 150px–300px image for the 32×32 favicon).

The Customizer (Site Identity) does not have this problem. For an exact 512×512 image it still sends the image through `crop-image` with `context: 'site-icon'`, which creates the `cropped-` attachment with all site icon sizes. The two UIs give different results for the same image.

This has been the behaviour since the Site Icon setting was added to Settings > General in 6.5 (#54370). It is still present in trunk.

== Steps to reproduce ==

 1. On a fresh install, go to Settings > General.
 2. Click "Choose a Site Icon" and upload/select a PNG that is exactly 512×512.
 3. Note that no cropper appears. Save Changes.
 4. Inspect the attachment and the icon URLs:
{{{
wp post meta get $(wp option get site_icon) _wp_attachment_metadata --format=json
wp eval 'foreach ( array( 32, 180, 192, 270, 512 ) as $s ) { echo $s, ": ", get_site_icon_url( $s ), PHP_EOL; }'
}}}
 5. Repeat with a square image of any other size (e.g. 1024×1024). The cropper appears, and after cropping the `site_icon-*` sizes exist.

== Expected result ==

The site icon attachment has the 32, 180, 192 and 270 sizes, and `get_site_icon_url( 32 )` returns a 32×32 file, matching what happens in the Customizer or with any non-512 image.

== Actual result ==

The attachment has only the standard intermediate sizes (thumbnail/medium). `get_site_icon_url()` returns the nearest larger size for every requested size, e.g.:
{{{
32:  .../icon-150x150.png
180: .../icon-300x300.png
192: .../icon-300x300.png
270: .../icon-300x300.png
512: .../icon.png
}}}
`_wp_attachment_context` is not set to `site-icon`.

== Cause ==

`site-icon.js`, `select` handler ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/js/_enqueues/admin/site-icon.js#L118-L134 L118–134]): if the selected image already matches the required size, it calls `switchToUpdate()` and sets the hidden field to the original attachment ID, skipping the cropper entirely.

The site icon sizes are only added in `wp_ajax_crop_image()` for the `site-icon` context, via `WP_Site_Icon::additional_sizes()` on `intermediate_image_sizes_advanced` ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/wp-admin/includes/ajax-actions.php#L4092-L4119 ajax-actions.php L4092–4119]).

For comparison, the Customizer's `SiteIconControl.onSelect()` handles the exact-size case by still calling `crop-image` with a full-image crop ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/js/_enqueues/wp/customize/controls.js#L4874-L4900 controls.js L4874–4900]).


== Possible fixes ==

 * Match the Customizer: in `site-icon.js`, when the image is already 512×512, call `wp.ajax.post( 'crop-image', { context: 'site-icon', cropDetails: { x1: 0, y1: 0, width: 512, height: 512, dst_width: 512, dst_height: 512 } } )` instead of using the original attachment. This keeps the existing "cropped-" duplicate behaviour discussed in #33011 / #38530.
 * Or, generate the site icon sizes on the selected attachment without creating a duplicate (e.g. when the `site_icon` option is saved), so both UIs produce the same result.

== Related ==

#54370, #33011, #38530, #36441, #58137

summary: Editor: Support spacing presets for text indent

- wp_apply_typography_support() generates its styles with convert_vars_to_classnames, which drops preset values that have no classname. Spacing presets have no classnames, so text indent is generated in a separate style engine call. Without this, text indent presets are lost on the front end for server-rendered blocks.

summary: WP_Http_Cookie accepts cookies with an empty or missing name
_description:
When a `WP_Http_Cookie` is created from a header string, an empty or missing name is not treated as invalid:

 * `=abc; path=/` results in `name = ''` and `value = 'abc'`. `test()` only checks for a `null` name, so it returns `true`, and `getHeaderValue()` returns `=abc`.
 * A pair without `=` (e.g. `novalue`) results in `name = ''` and `value = 'ovalue'`: `strpos()` returns `false`, so the first character of the value is cut off.
 * An array with `'name' => ''` behaves the same way.

RFC 6265 (section 5.2) says to ignore a cookie with an empty name or without `=`. The newer RFC 6265bis draft keeps such cookies, but treats `novalue` as an empty name with the value `novalue`. Either way, `ovalue` is wrong.

This came up in review of [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13983 PR 13983] (PHPStan, #65817). That PR makes `WP_Http::normalize_cookies()` skip cookies without a name, without a value, or with a non-scalar value, so they are no longer sent through Requests. `WP_Http::buildCookieHeader()`, which is still used by `WP_Http_Curl` and `WP_Http_Streams`, can still send `=abc`.

Leaving `name` as `null` in the constructor for these cases would treat them as invalid without throwing an exception.

Related: #12761 (whitespace-only cookie pairs in the same parsing code).

summary: Make all admin notices render after the main H1 heading
_description:
Related: #50486 / [64282]

Many important admin notices (see a few examples in the attached screenshot) render before the page main H1 heading.

I do realize they are rendered at the very top of the page to be visually prominent. However, this has a few important disadvantages:

- These notices may be entirely missed by screen reader users, as they come after the main H1 heading. Many users may jump directly to the H1 and miss anything that comes before it.
- It's not a case that an important accessibility best practice requires the main H1 heading to be the very first thing inside the `<main>` element.
- These notices aren't moved to the `<aside>` element added in #50486. As such, they are separated from other notices and aren't included in an ARIA landmark.

Basically, to my understanding, all the notices hooked to:

- network_admin_notices
- user_admin_notices
- admin_notices
- all_admin_notices

stay before the main H1 heading ''if'' they use the additional CSS class `inline`.

It is worth reminding that the admin notices that ''do not'' use the `inline` CSS class are moved via Javascript ''after'' the H1.

I'd like to propose to remove the `inline` CSS class from all these notices.

Visual prominence can be achieved by other means, for example with a good usage of white space.

This proposal is not related to 'inline' notices that are ''intentionally'' rendered in the middle of the page.

wp_set_object_terms() leaves term_order at 0 for newly added terms in sorted taxonomies when term counting is deferred
_description:
For a taxonomy registered with `'sort' => true`, `wp_set_object_terms()` is meant to store terms in the order they are passed. When term counting is deferred and a term is added to an object that already has terms, the new term is left at the column default `term_order = 0`. It then sorts ahead of the existing terms instead of after them.

The wrong value is written to `wp_term_relationships` so the order of terms is destroyed.

=== Steps to reproduce ===

Add this MU plugin to a site. It registers a sorted taxonomy and defers term counting.

{{{#!php
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Term order bug reproduction
 * Description: Registers a sorted taxonomy and defers term counting, to reproduce the `term_order` bug in `wp_set_object_terms()`.
 */

add_action(
	'init',
	static function () {
		register_taxonomy(
			'byline',
			'post',
			array(
				'label'        => 'Byline Author',
				'sort'         => true,
				'args'         => array( 'orderby' => 'term_order' ),
				'show_in_rest' => true,
			)
		);

		wp_defer_term_counting( true );
	}
);
}}}

Then, in wp-admin:

   1. Go to Posts > Byline Author and create three terms: `Alice`, `Bob` and `Charlie`.
   2. Create a new post.
   3. From the Quick Edit panel, add `Alice`, then `Bob` to Byline Authors and save the post.
   4. Add `Charlie` in the same panel, after `Bob`. Save the post again.
   5. Check the Byline Authors again from the Quick Edit Panel

Result: `Chalie, Alice, Bob`

Expected: `Alice, Bob, Charlie`

See Video: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9c91783e-ecd6-4201-84de-e99e2bf08819

For sorted taxonomies, `wp_set_object_terms()` reads the object's terms again before it assigns `term_order`, and only numbers the terms it finds in that read.

That read is cached. Normally the term count update clears the cache before the read happens. When term counting is deferred, nothing clears it, so the read returns the old list without the newly added term. The new term is skipped and keeps `term_order = 0`.

`wp_set_object_terms()` does clear the cache itself, but only after this read. That was added in #40306.

We hit this during a bulk content migration. We turned off term counting for the whole run with `wp_defer_term_counting( true )` to improve migration speed. Byline authors were stored in a sorted taxonomy, and on posts with more than one author the byline order came out wrong.

summary: Taxonomy: Add description to the fields searched by WP_Term_Query / admin term search
_description:
`WP_Term_Query::get_search_sql()` hardcodes its `search` matching to
just two columns:

{{{
return $wpdb->prepare( '((t.name LIKE %s) OR (t.slug LIKE %s))', $like, $like );
}}}

A term's `description` (stored on `wp_term_taxonomy`) is never
considered, even though:

- `wp_term_taxonomy` is already unconditionally `INNER JOIN`ed into
  every term query (it's where `taxonomy`, `parent`, and `count` come
  from too), so no new join is required to reach `description`.
- A `description__like` arg already exists for exact-field LIKE
  matching — it's just never combined with `search`.

Because `edit-tags.php?taxonomy=X` is the single shared admin screen
for every taxonomy (Categories, Tags, Link Categories, and any custom
taxonomy with an admin UI all use the same `WP_Terms_List_Table`
class), this affects all of them identically: searching the admin
term list only matches name/slug, never description, with no way to
opt in short of hooking `terms_clauses` and hand-building a `tt.description
LIKE` clause in a plugin.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Create a category (or tag) with a short, generic name but a
   distinctive description, e.g. name "Misc", description containing
   the word "pineapple".
2. Go to Posts > Categories (or Posts > Tags) in wp-admin.
3. Search for "pineapple".

Expected: the term is found, since "pineapple" appears in its
description.

Actual: no results — only `name`/`slug` are searched.

Suggested fix: add an opt-in `search_columns` query var to
`WP_Term_Query` (accepting `'name'`, `'slug'`, `'description'`;
default empty array, preserving today's name+slug-only behavior for
every existing caller), and have `get_search_sql()` build its `OR`'d
`LIKE` clause from the configured columns instead of the hardcoded
pair — mirroring the existing `user_search_columns` pattern already
used by `WP_User_Query`. `WP_Terms_List_Table::prepare_items()` then
opts in to all three columns for the admin search box (both the
`get_terms()` call and the `wp_count_terms()` pagination count, so the
displayed total stays consistent with the actual results).

summary: Category Search Fails When Search Term Contains an Ampersand Followed by a Space, Admin Page/Post Editor
_description:
Bug Report: 

Product: WordPress  
Version: 7.1.2, 7.1.3 and others  
Component: Posts / Categories / Editor  
Issue Type: Bug

**Summary**

When adding or editing a post in the WordPress admin dashboard, searching for a category whose name contains an ampersand (`&`) followed by a space does not return the expected search result.

For example, a category named **“Tour & Travel”** cannot be found when searching for `Tour & ` (including the trailing space).

## Steps to Reproduce

2. Navigate to **Posts → Add New** or edit an existing post.
3. Open the Categories panel in the post editor.
4. Search for `Tour & `, including the space after the ampersand.
5. Observe the search results.

## Expected Behavior

The category **“Tour & Travel”** should appear in the search results when searching for `Tour & `, since the entered text matches the beginning of the category name.

## Actual Behavior

The category does not appear in the search results when the search term contains an ampersand followed by a space.

## Additional Information

- The issue occurs in the WordPress admin post editor while adding or editing a post.
- The affected category contains an ampersand followed by a space in its name.
- The issue appears to involve partial category-name matching when special characters and whitespace are present.

**Suggested investigation:** Check how the category search filters and processes search terms containing ampersands and trailing whitespace, including any differences in query tokenization or sanitization.

## Impact

This behavior makes it harder for users to find and assign categories containing ampersands when searching by partial category name.

summary: Notes: Add a filter for the emoji a note can be reacted with
_description:
Follow up to https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10930 - emoji reactions on Notes ship with a fixed set of five emoji. This adds a way for sites to change that set.

''Claude wrote the rest of this ticket; I checked it against the code:''

> Reactions accept a fixed set of five emoji (heart, celebration, smile, eyes, rocket). Right now the list is hardcoded in a private `WP_REST_Comments_Controller::get_note_reaction_keys()` method, so a site can't add an emoji its team uses, remove one that doesn't fit, or turn reactions off.
>
> The proposed change:
>
>  * Add a `wp_note_reaction_emojis` filter. Each entry has a `hexKey` (the emoji's code points in hex, eg. `1f984` for the unicorn) and a translatable `label`. Returning an empty array turns off adding reactions. Existing reactions still show and their authors can still remove them.
>  * Add `wp_get_note_reaction_emojis()` and `wp_get_note_reaction_keys()`, plus `wp_normalize_note_reaction_key()`, which normalizes filtered keys the same way reactions are stored: lowercase, padded to four digits, U+FE0F dropped. Malformed keys, surrogates, values past U+10FFFF, empty labels and duplicate keys are dropped.
>  * The REST API validates reactions against the filtered list instead of the hardcoded one.
>  * The list is passed to the editor as the `noteReactionEmojis` block editor setting, so the reaction menu offers exactly the emoji the server accepts.
>
> Example:
>
> {{{#!php
> <?php
> add_filter( 'wp_note_reaction_emojis', function ( $emojis ) {
> 	$emojis[] = array(
> 		'hexKey' => '1f984',
> 		'label'  => __( 'unicorn', 'my-plugin' ),
> 	);
> 	return $emojis;
> } );
> }}}
>
> The filter docs note that the editor renders emoji as text, so newer emoji and flags may not display on every system. Choosing emoji that work for a site's users is left to the site for now.
>
> Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84200
>
> The patch is stacked on the backport (https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/10930) and needs that to land first.

Comments: "Mine" view count not updated via AJAX after moderation actions
_description:
On the Comments screen (edit-comments.php), performing an AJAX moderation
action — Approve, Unapprove, Spam, Trash, Delete Permanently, or Undo —
live-updates several of the view tab counts in the DOM without a full page
reload. `edit-comments.js`'s `delAfter` handler bumps:

- `span.all-count`
- `span.pending-count` (via `updatePending()`)
- `span.approved-count` (via `updateApproved()`)
- `span.spam-count`
- `span.trash-count`

`span.mine-count` is never touched by this code. As a result, after e.g.
trashing or deleting one of your own comments via the inline row actions,
the "Mine (N)" tab keeps showing the old count until the page is fully
reloaded — inconsistent with every other tab, which updates immediately.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Log in as a user who has left at least one comment on the site
   (comment's `user_id` matches the logged-in user).
2. Go to Comments in wp-admin. Note the "Mine (N)" count in the view tabs.
3. Click the "Mine" tab to filter to your own comments.
4. Use the inline "Trash" (or "Delete Permanently" / "Approve" / etc.) link
   on one of your own comments.

Expected: "Mine (N)" decrements immediately, matching how "All" and
"Trash" update.

Actual: "Mine (N)" stays at its old value until the page is reloaded.

Root cause: "Mine" uses the same status scope as "All" (approved +
pending comments; see `WP_Comments_List_Table::get_views()`, which queries
with no `status` arg and defaults to `'all'`), just filtered to the
current user's own comments via `user_id`. The AJAX handler updates "All"
but has no way to know, client-side, whether the affected comment belongs
to the current user, so it was never extended to also update "Mine".

Suggested fix: render a `data-comment-user-id` attribute on each comment
row (`WP_Comments_List_Table::single_row()`), localize the current user's
ID to the `admin-comments` script, and in `edit-comments.js` compare the
two to decide whether to also bump `span.mine-count` alongside
`span.all-count` for the same `pendingDiff`/`approvedDiff` changes.
