summary: Fix DOM and visual order mismatch in the various media dialogs
_description:
In the various media dialog, the buttons in the top toolbar come first in the DOM order but they are visually placed after the main dialog heading on the left.

This introduces a mismatch between the DOM order and visual order that is an accessibility barrier for screen reader users. Note that this has nothing to do with Tab keyboard navigation. Rather, it's about navigating content with arrows keys or other screen readers navigation mechanisms (e.g. 'read all').

Worth also noting that any other software will get the order mismatch, including AI agents.

For example in the Media Library 'Edit attachments' modal dialog, the `edit-media-header` element, which contains the 3 buttons Previous, Next, and Close, comes before the `media-frame-title` element, which contains the H1 heading. As such, when navigating content following the DOM source there is a mismatch between the DOM and the visual order.

Same in the media dialog, where the `media-modal-close` button is before the H1 heading in the DOM.

It's also worth noting that now that initial focus is set on the modal dialog element, there is no need for the buttons to be the first thing within the dialog.

summary: Block Supports: Add PHP helpers for generating styles and classes when serialization is skipped
_description:
This ticket tracks backporting changes from Gutenberg to WordPress Core.

Gutenberg PRs:
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84207
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84205
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84208
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84206
https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84209

It adds a PHP helper for each of the border, shadow, spacing, color and background block supports, wp_get_border_classes_and_styles() and so on, mirroring the JS getBorderClassesAndStyles() family. Each takes block attributes and returns the support's class and style. The block supports now build their output with these helpers, and blocks that skip serialization can use them instead of rebuilding styles by hand.

Avatar, Post Featured Image, Icon, Post Navigation Link, Navigation Submenu, Comment Author Avatar, Calendar and Button currently copy parts of this logic, and the copies have drifted. Those blocks move onto the helpers when the Gutenberg package is next updated.

This is a behaviour-preserving change, so the block support output should be identical to before. It depends on https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/13491 (background clip) landing first.

summary: Blocks: Add asset file (.asset.php) support for styles in register_block_style_handle()
_description:
In `block.json`, block metadata fields like `style`, `editorStyle`, and `viewStyle` accept file paths via the `file:` prefix (e.g. `"style": "file:./style.css"`). Build tools such as `@wordpress/scripts` and Webpack generate adjacent `.asset.php` files containing automated cache-busting hashes/versions and dependencies.

While `register_block_script_handle()` and `register_block_script_module_id()` detect and load adjacent `.asset.php` files to extract custom handle names, dependencies, and versions, `register_block_style_handle()` previously did not look for an `.asset.php` file, hardcoding dependencies to `array()` and ignoring asset versions or custom handles.

Follows up on Gutenberg issue [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/56838 #56838] (matching the work done for scripts in #60485).

A PR has been prepared with full unit test coverage:
https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/14065

summary: GD image editor saves resized indexed PNGs as truecolor (regression since 3.5)
_description:
== Summary ==

This is the GD follow-up to #36477 (see comment:62 and comment:63), where the Imagick side was fixed in [59589].

Since 3.5, the GD editor saves every resized sub-size of an indexed (color type 3) PNG as truecolor RGBA. Sub-sizes are often several times larger than the original.

In 3.4, `image_resize()` did this:

{{{#!php
<?php
if ( IMAGETYPE_PNG == $orig_type && function_exists('imageistruecolor') && !imageistruecolor( $image ) )
	imagetruecolortopalette( $newimage, false, imagecolorstotal( $image ) );
}}}

It checked the original image and converted the new one. [22094] moved this into `WP_Image_Editor_GD::_save()`, which checks the image being saved. `_resize()` always returns a truecolor image from `wp_imagecreatetruecolor()`, so for sub-sizes the check is always false and the conversion never runs.

== Steps to reproduce ==

1. `add_filter( 'wp_image_editors', fn() => array( 'WP_Image_Editor_GD' ) );`
2. Upload `tests/phpunit/data/images/png-tests/cloudflare-status.png`.
3. Check the sub-sizes' PNG color type: all are 6 (RGBA). Expected: 3 (indexed).

== Results ==

Core's png-tests fixtures, trunk editor classes, PHP 8.3, libgd 2.3.3. Percentages are sub-size bytes relative to the original upload, averaged across generated sizes, with the worst single size in brackets.

||= Fixture =||= Transparency =||= Trunk =||= Patched =||
|| cloudflare-status.png || none || 405% (707%) || 110% (189%) ||
|| Palette_icon-or8.png || none || 195% (359%) || 78% (140%) ||
|| test8.png || binary || 261% (413%) || unchanged ||
|| deskcat8.png || partial || 226% (424%) || unchanged ||

Patched output is visually indistinguishable from trunk (PSNR ~39 dB vs. the truecolor output).

== Scope: opaque images only ==

`imagetruecolortopalette()` discards alpha on libgd 2.3.3, even for a minimal two-color image with `imagealphablending( false )` and `imagesavealpha( true )`. Transparent regions become opaque. Preserving transparency would need a per-pixel loop in PHP, which isn't practical on large images. So the patch converts only indexed sources with no transparency, and leaves transparent ones as they are today.

== Proposed patch ==

* In `load()`, record whether the source is palette-based and whether it has any transparency (`imagecolortransparent()` index or non-zero alpha in the palette).
* In `_save()` for `image/png`, when the source was an opaque palette image, convert a copy of the image to a 256-color palette and save that.
* Convert a copy, not `$image` itself: converting in place makes a later WebP/AVIF save from the same editor fail (0-byte file), since GD can't write those from palette images (see performance#2018).
* Unit tests: opaque indexed fixture stays indexed after resize; transparent indexed fixture keeps its alpha; PNG then WebP save from the same editor both succeed.

Related: #36477, #30402, #63448, #53408

summary: AVIF uploads get JPEG sub-sizes when Imagick (ImageMagick 6) reports the file as HEIC
_description:
Hi everyone,

I searched the existing tickets before posting and didn't find anything that matches this exactly. Related are #53645 (HEIC to JPEG conversion in 6.7) and #62365 (HEIC mapping vs. `image_editor_output_format` overrides), but as far as I can tell they cover real HEIC uploads, not AVIF files. If this is a duplicate, please point me to the right ticket.

== Summary ==

On a server with ImageMagick 6.9.11, uploaded AVIF files get their sub-sizes (thumbnail, medium) generated as JPEG instead of AVIF. The reason seems to be that Imagick identifies the AVIF file as HEIC, so the HEIC to JPEG mapping kicks in.

== Environment ==

 * WordPress 7.1.3, fresh install, no content
 * PHP 8.5.9
 * Imagick 3.8.1 with ImageMagick 6.9.11-60 Q16
 * GD (bundled) with AVIF support
 * Theme: Twenty Twenty-Five

== Is this the latest version? ==

Yes, I tested on a fresh install of 7.1.3.

== Does it happen with all plugins deactivated and a default theme? ==

Yes. The install is new, Twenty Twenty-Five is active and no plugins are active. Debug logging is enabled and nothing is written to the log. `image_editor_output_format` and `image_editor_default_mime_type` have no filters attached.

== Steps to reproduce ==

 1. Use a server where `WP_Image_Editor_Imagick` is selected (ImageMagick 6.9.11, AVIF listed in the supported formats).
 2. Upload an AVIF file to the Media Library.
 3. Look at the attachment metadata (`wp_get_attachment_metadata()`) or the uploads folder.

== Expected result ==

The original stays `image/avif` and the sub-sizes are generated as AVIF (e.g. `image-150x150.avif`).

== Actual result ==

The original is stored as `image/avif`, but the sub-sizes are created as JPEG (`image-150x150.jpg`, `"mime-type": "image/jpeg"` in the metadata).

== What I found when debugging ==

 * `wp_get_image_mime( $file )` returns `image/avif`, and so does `get_post_mime_type()`.
 * `new Imagick( $file )` reports `getImageFormat()` = `HEIC` and `getImageMimeType()` = `image/x-heic` for this AVIF file.
 * After `wp_get_image_editor( $file )`, the editor's `mime_type` property is `image/heic`.
 * Calling `$editor->save( $path, 'image/avif' )` explicitly works fine and writes a valid AVIF. So Imagick can encode AVIF, the problem only occurs in the normal upload flow where no target type is passed.
 * Site Health lists the default transforms `image/heic → image/jpeg` (plus heif and the sequence types).

My guess is that ImageMagick 6 handles AVIF through the libheif delegate and therefore labels it as HEIC. WordPress then seems to take the type from Imagick instead of from the file itself, and the default HEIC to JPEG mapping is applied to what is really an AVIF file. I haven't looked deeper into the code than this, so please correct me if I'm wrong.

== Workaround ==

Forcing GD fixes it, since GD reports the format correctly:

{{{
add_filter( 'wp_image_editors', fn() => [ 'WP_Image_Editor_GD' ] );
}}}

With that filter, new uploads get AVIF sub-sizes after regenerating thumbnails.

== Possible direction ==

Maybe the editor could use the mime type detected from the file (`wp_get_image_mime()`) when Imagick returns a HEIC type for a file that WordPress itself identifies as AVIF. ImageMagick 6.9.11 is old, so this may be an edge case, but it is still shipped by some distributions and hosts.

Thanks for taking a look. I can provide a sample AVIF file and more test output if that helps.

summary: Comments: Hide zero-count status filters on the Comments list table
_description:
The Posts list table (`WP_Posts_List_Table::get_views()`) hides any status
filter link — other than "All" — whose post count is zero:

{{{
if ( ! in_array( $status_name, $avail_post_stati, true ) || empty( $num_posts->$status_name ) ) {
	continue;
}
}}}

`WP_Comments_List_Table::get_views()` has no equivalent check. As a result,
"Pending", "Approved", "Spam", "Trash", and "Mine" are always rendered as
filter links above the Comments list table, even when their count is `(0)`.

On a typical site with few or no pending/spam/trashed comments, this clutters
the screen with filter links that lead to an empty list, rather than only
showing filters that are actually useful.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Go to a site where every comment is approved (no pending, spam, or
   trashed comments).
2. Go to Comments in wp-admin.
3. Observe the filter row above the list: "All | Mine | Pending (0) |
   Approved (12) | Spam (0) | Trash (0)".

Expected behavior: filters with a zero count, other than "All", should not
be shown — consistent with how the Posts list table already behaves for
post statuses.

summary: Introduce WHATWG-compliant encoding name canonicalization.
_description:
WordPress largely treats character encoding names in an agnostic fashion, passing them off to browsers, `iconv()`, and `mb_convert_encoding()` transparently. This can lead to confusing data flow for text data, particularly because it’s unclear how arbitrary text coming into WordPress will be handled.

The [https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/ ENCODING spec] defines which character encodings should be supported by web-integrating systems and which variations of each encoding’s name should be treated as equivalent aliases.

For example, while `l1` and `us-ascii` are both treated by browsers as `windows-1252`, they are never recognized as such within WordPress. In fact, since `mb_convert_encoding()` and `iconv()` don’t follow this interoperability standard, they fail for a number of supported encodings.

As WordPress moves towards deprecating non-UTF-8 support (#62172), it should provide robust mechanisms for converting text at the boundaries of input and output to aid this transition.

Prior work normalized UTF-8 detection in #61182, but focused on the detection of `UTF-8` specifically, and without taking into account the additional encodings in the WHATWG standard.

Further work should provide standards-compliant canonicalization while being explicit which set of supported charsets is being detected. For instance, the set of `mysql` charset names is disjoint from the set of web standard charset names.

=== Activities requiring ENCODING support.

 - Decoding full HTML documents.
 - Reading and writing emails.
 - Printing `<meta charset>` tags.
 - Inferring MIME content type.

== Related work

 - #64427 inferring MIME content type.

summary: Toolbar: same W and site name behavior in the admin, the editors and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes two fixed links in the Toolbar. The W always goes to the Dashboard. The site name always goes to the site. Both work the same in the admin, in the editors and on the front end.

It replaces #66235, which covered only the site name.

== Current behavior ==

The W and the site name are the first two items of the Toolbar.

 * A click on the W goes to the About WordPress page. It is the first item of the Toolbar, and it goes to a page people rarely need.
 * A click on the site name changes with the place. In the admin it goes to the site. On the front end it goes to the Dashboard.
 * The site name menu also changes. In the admin it has only Visit Site. On the front end it has Dashboard, Plugins and Themes.
 * When the site has no site icon, the icon changes too. It is a house in the admin and a gauge on the front end.

Since 7.1 the Toolbar is also displayed in the editors. There, the Toolbar has no link to the Dashboard. The W goes to the About page and the site name goes to the site.

== Proposal ==

'''The W'''

 * Click: the W always goes to the Dashboard.
 * Menu: Dashboard is the first item. The other items stay the same.
 * Small screens: the W stays visible. Today it is hidden under 600px.

[[Image(toolbar-w-menu.png)]]

'''The site name'''

 * Click: the site name always goes to the site.
 * Menu: the same items everywhere. Visit Site, Plugins and Themes. On multisite, Manage Site comes right after Visit Site.
 * Icon: the site icon when the site has one, as it works since 7.1. When the site has no site icon, the same default icon everywhere.

[[Image(toolbar-site-name-menu.png)]]

The Dashboard has one place, under the W. It leaves the site name menu.

Small screens:

[[Image(toolbar-small-screens.png)]]

== Why ==

 * The W gets a useful click. The logo in the top left corner is the most visible item of the Toolbar. I believe people expect it to go to the home of the admin. About WordPress is still in the menu, one click away.
 * The W menu keeps its role. It still holds the links about WordPress. Only the click changes.
 * One click to the Dashboard from everywhere. This matters most in the editors, where the Toolbar has no way back to the Dashboard today.
 * One behavior to learn. Each item does one thing. People don't need to check where they are before they click.
 * Two clear places. The W is the admin and the site name is the site. Today one item switches between both.
 * It works on multisite. My Sites stays next to the W, as today. In the Network Admin, the W goes to the network Dashboard.
 * **Better on touch screens**. A tap on the site name opens the menu. Today, in the admin, that menu has a single item.

== Accessibility ==

 * The accessible name of the W becomes "Dashboard". Today it is "About WordPress". The name says where the link goes.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change.
 * Both menus have the same items in the same order everywhere. It is more predictable for screen reader users.
 * The site icon is decorative. The site name stays next to it.

== Backward compatibility ==

 * Two clicks change. The W goes to the Dashboard and not to the About page. On the front end, the site name goes to the site and not to the Dashboard.
 * The Dashboard item moves from the site name menu to the W menu. It keeps its ID.
 * People only see the items they have access to, same as today.
 * Classic themes keep their extra items (Widgets, Menus, Background and Header) after Themes.
 * The other menu items keep their IDs. Plugins that add items to these menus keep working.
 * Under 600px the Toolbar gets one more item, the W.

== Related ==

 * #66235 is the first version of this proposal, only for the site name. I will close it in favor of this ticket.
 * #28398 and #19184 asked for fixed links years ago and were closed. Since then, the site name got the site icon and the Toolbar is displayed in the editors.
 * #65088 site icon in the Toolbar.
 * #65091 Toolbar in the Site Editor and Block Editor.

summary: Theme installer: Themes can be previewed even when the Preview button is disabled
_description:
In the Theme installer at `wp-admin/theme-install.php` the action buttons for the themes that can't be previewed, for example because they are incompatible with the current WP version or the current PHP version, are disabled.

This is intentional to prevent users from installing / activating / previewing an incompatible theme.

However, clicking on any part of the Theme card outside of the buttons still gives access to the Theme preview (note that the Preview and the Live Preview are two different things).

This is unexpected and should be fixed.

To reproduce, the quick way:
- In `src/wp-includes/functions.php` make the two functions `is_wp_version_compatible()` and `is_php_version_compatible()` return `false` early.
- Go to the Theme installer.
- Observe the theme cards have their buttons disabled. The button labels are for example: Cannot Install / Preview, Cannot Activate / Live Preview.
- For a non-installed theme (one that shows the Cannot Install / Preview buttons) click on any part of the theme's card outside of the buttons.
- Observe it brings you to the Theme preview.
- For an installed theme (one that has the Cannot Activate / Live Preview buttons), click on any part of the theme's card outside of the buttons.
- Observe it brings you to the Theme preview.

So for both installed and non-installed theme shown in the Theme installer, clicking the theme's card still gives access to the theme's Preview.

summary: No way to turn off importing alt text from image XMP metadata
_description:
This is a follow-up to issue #63895.  The fix for that issue created a new `wp_get_image_alttext()` function which parses images for XMP metadata and uses that to populate the alt text for the image.  Currently `wp_get_image_alttext()` is called unconditionally - if you don't want this functionality, there does not appear to be any way to turn it off.  You could use the `wp_read_image_metadata` filter to overwrite the alt text after `wp_get_image_alttext()` has already run, but it would be better to have a way to prevent `wp_get_image_alttext()` from running a bunch of unnecessary code in the first place.

I will submit a pull request to address this.

summary: Admin: Button styles are not consistent in active-while-focused states
_description:
r46241 (#34904) added styles which remove the focus ring while a button is active by assigning {{{box-shadow: none}}} to {{{.button:active}}}. This effect can be seen when activating buttons like "Search Posts" on the Posts screen.

**Bug:** Not all buttons apply this consistently, for example the "Save Changes" button on the Settings > General screen maintains the focus ring while active.

**Technical Analysis:**

[https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L84 Secondary buttons] and [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L52 buttons forced active with the .active class] hide the focus ring, while [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L32-L36 plain (primary) buttons] and [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/aee05d91bb71c9c757125e5bf82088d097af8131/src/wp-admin/css/colors/_mixins.scss#L119-L123 tertiary buttons] have no corresponding style. These styles are used in generating color scheme stylesheets that are loaded after the base styles from {{{buttons.css}}}, and take priority over the base styles.

**Resolution:**

Adding {{{box-shadow: none}}} consistently to all of the button mixins would likely be the expected resolution given the current state of button styling.

In parallel, Gutenberg's [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/84090 GB#84090] discusses general styling updates for this state which may ultimately make current assumptions obsolete, but does not block consistency improvements in the meantime.

summary: Taxonomy: Repeated hierarchy decoding slows hierarchical term queries
_description:
get_term_children() calls _get_term_hierarchy() at each recursive step. The hierarchy option may already be in the object cache, but get_option() still unserializes the complete map on every read. WP_Term_Query's hierarchical hide_empty pass repeats the traversal for each empty parent.

This can make ordinary category lists slow even when SQL is cheap. A local fixture with 8,000 terms in a balanced tree (up to four children per parent, empty parents and nonempty leaves) needed 12,182 hierarchy reads to build one list. Only two SQL queries were executed. The fixture has one published post assigned to the leaves of each taxonomy; it is a controlled fixture rather than a production-site measurement.

PHP 8.3.0, MariaDB 11.4, OPcache enabled in both versions. Medians of five alternating runs:

|| Operation || Terms || Before || After ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 1,000 || 0.116 s || 0.030 s ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 4,000 || 1.706 s || 0.131 s ||
|| wp_list_categories() || 8,000 || 6.909 s || 0.227 s ||
|| WP_Query including descendants || 8,000 || 1.269 s || 0.152 s ||

The option cache was warmed before timing. Each measurement used a fresh PHP process, so the term-query result cache was cold. WordPress bootstrap was excluded from the timer. List HTML, returned terms and post IDs matched between versions in all 90 measurements.

To reproduce the path, create a sizeable hierarchical taxonomy with empty parents and posts assigned to its leaves, then time these calls in separate requests without a pre-existing term-query result cache:

{{{#!php
$start = microtime( true );
$html = wp_list_categories( array(
    'taxonomy' => 'category',
    'echo' => false,
    'title_li' => '',
) );
$elapsed = microtime( true ) - $start;
}}}

The proposed change passes an already loaded hierarchy into the existing descendant traversal and reuses that hierarchy within the hide_empty pass, keyed by taxonomy. No persistent or request-global cache is introduced. A warm term-query result cache bypasses the affected hide_empty processing, so the same gain should not be expected on cache hits.

Eight regression tests cover ordering, invalid taxonomies, leaves, insertion/reparenting/deletion between calls, descendants excluded from the result set, multiple taxonomies and hierarchy read counts. All eight pass with the patch; the two read-count tests fail without it. The broader term, category and query/taxQuery groups complete 753 tests and 1,933 assertions with no failures. One pre-existing PHPUnit warning also appears on the original code; strict --fail-on-warning runs exit nonzero.

Compatibility point for review: option filters are called fewer times. A get_term callback that changes hierarchy relationships during the same hide_empty pass may observe the pass's existing hierarchy snapshot. Changes between separate calls are covered by tests.

summary: Show plugin translation completion and allow managing installed language packs
_description:
**Summary**
Improve translation management for installed plugins by showing translation availability and completion status directly on the Plugins → Installed Plugins screen, and allow administrators to remove unnecessary installed plugin language packs.

**Problem**

WordPress automatically downloads and updates translation packages for plugins when translations are available for the site's installed languages.
However, administrators currently have very little visibility or control over these plugin translations from the WordPress admin interface.

For an installed plugin, the administrator cannot easily see:
- which plugin translations are currently installed;
- how complete a translation is for a particular locale;
- whether a translation package is available but not installed;
- whether a translation is incomplete;
- which translation packages are no longer needed on the site;
- how to remove an unnecessary translation package without manually working with files in wp-content/languages/plugins/.

This becomes especially noticeable on multilingual sites, development environments, migrated sites, or sites where the active locale configuration has changed over time.
As a result, unused translation files may remain installed, while administrators have no convenient way to understand their status or manage them.

**Proposed solution**

Add a translation management interface for each plugin on the Installed Plugins screen.
For example, a new action such as:
Translations
could open an expandable section, modal, or another suitable interface showing available locales for the plugin.
Example:
Contact Form 7
Translations:
{{{
Ukrainian (uk)     100% translated    Installed
German (de_DE)      96% translated    Installed    [Remove]
Polish (pl_PL)      84% translated    Not installed
Spanish (es_ES)    100% translated    Installed    [Remove]
}}}

The exact UI could be discussed separately, but the important information would be:
- locale / language name;
- translation completion percentage;
- whether a language pack is available;
- whether it is currently installed;
- when appropriate, an action to remove the installed language pack.
Translation completion percentage
It would be useful to expose the translation completion percentage because the current state is otherwise difficult to understand.
For example:

{{{
Ukrainian — 100%
German — 96%
Polish — 84%
}}}

This gives the administrator much more useful information than simply knowing that a translation exists.
It also helps explain why a particular plugin may still contain untranslated strings even though a translation package is installed.
Ideally, this information could be obtained from the WordPress.org translation infrastructure.
If the current translations API does not expose the translation completion percentage, this may require an associated WordPress.org Meta / Translation API change.
Managing installed language packs
Administrators should also be able to remove unnecessary plugin translation packages from WordPress admin.
Currently this generally requires direct filesystem access and knowledge of files stored under:

{{{
wp-content/languages/plugins/
}}}

A simple Remove translation action would make this functionality accessible without requiring FTP, SSH, hosting file managers, or manual file deletion.
The action should only remove the translation package for the selected locale and plugin.
It should not:
- remove the plugin;
- change the site's locale;
- remove translations for other plugins;
- affect translations bundled directly inside the plugin.

**Possible use cases**
1. Site language was changed
A site previously used several locales and later switched to another language.
Old plugin translation packages may remain installed even though they are no longer required.

2. Multilingual development site
During development or testing, several languages may be temporarily installed.
After testing is finished, administrators should be able to remove translations that are no longer needed.

3. Understanding incomplete translations
A plugin may appear partially untranslated.
Displaying the completion percentage would help administrators understand whether this is caused by an incomplete community translation rather than by a problem with WordPress or the plugin itself.

4. Better transparency
WordPress currently downloads plugin translations automatically, but the process is mostly invisible to site administrators.
Providing translation information directly in the plugin management interface would make this behaviour easier to understand.

**Possible UI location**

One possible implementation would be to add a new plugin row action:
Settings | Deactivate | Translations
Selecting Translations could expand a secondary row underneath the plugin, similar to other plugin information displayed on this screen.
Another possibility would be a dedicated modal or details screen.
The exact UI is less important than providing access to the information and management actions.

**Scope**

This proposal is mainly about:
1. displaying plugin translation information in WordPress admin;
2. exposing translation completion status where possible;
3. showing which plugin language packs are installed;
4. allowing administrators to remove unnecessary plugin language packs.
The proposal does not suggest changing how translations themselves are created or approved on translate.wordpress.org.

Technical considerations

WordPress already has infrastructure for:
- discovering installed translations;
- downloading language packs;
- updating language packs;
- removing plugin translations when a plugin itself is deleted.

Therefore, much of the underlying language-pack functionality already exists.
The main additions would likely involve:
- exposing this information in the Installed Plugins UI;
- providing a safe action for deleting a specific plugin language pack;
- obtaining translation completion information from WordPress.org where available.
If translation completion percentages are not currently exposed by the WordPress.org translation API, that part may require a related WordPress.org Meta ticket.

**Expected benefit**

This would make plugin translation management more transparent and give site administrators greater control over automatically installed language resources.
It would also make WordPress easier to manage on multilingual sites and help administrators distinguish between plugin issues and incomplete community translations.

summary: Integrate WordPress.org closed, suspended, and outdated plugins and themes API data into Core
_description:
WordPress.org Meta Trac ticket [#8447](https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8447) and WordPress.org PR [#1004](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/1004) updated the WordPress.org Plugin and Theme APIs to expose structured metadata when plugins or themes are:

1. **Closed / Removed / Suspended:** (`closed => true`, `status => 'closed'|'disabled'|'suspend'`, `closed_date`, `reason`, `reason_text`, `is_security => true|false`).
2. **Outdated / Abandoned:** (`is_outdated => true`, `outdated_notice => string`, tested beyond the last three major WordPress versions or not modified for more than two years).
3. **Inaccessible for Security Reasons:** (`is_security => true` or `reason => 'security-issue'`).

Currently, WordPress Core lacks visibility into this metadata. Site administrators may be unaware when an installed plugin or theme has been removed from the repository due to a critical security issue, closed at the author's request, or abandoned without updates. Furthermore, opening the details modal for a closed item triggers a generic `plugins_api_failed` error (`"An unexpected error occurred..."`) instead of explaining why the item is unavailable.

== Related Links & Prior Art

* **Meta Trac Ticket:** https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8447
* **WordPress.org Pull Request:** https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/1004


----


== Proposed Solution & Changes

This patch adds complete Core support for storing, displaying, and alerting administrators about closed, suspended, outdated, or security-withdrawn plugins and themes.

=== 1. Update Check & Transient Storage

**`wp-includes/update.php`**

* In `wp_update_plugins()`:

  * Preserve `closed`, `closed_date`, `closed_reason`, `reason`, `reason_text`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, and `outdated_notice` in both the `response` and `no_update` arrays of the `update_plugins` transient.
  * Populate standalone `closed` response items into `no_update`.

* In `wp_update_themes()`:

  * Preserve `closed`, `status`, `is_closed`, `is_suspended`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, `outdated_notice`, `closed_date`, and `reason` metadata in both the `response` and `no_update` arrays of the `update_themes` transient.

=== 2. Plugins List Table UI & Inline Notices

**`wp-admin/includes/update.php`** and **`wp-admin/includes/class-wp-plugins-list-table.php`**

* `wp_plugin_update_rows()` now processes items in `no_update` when they are flagged as closed or outdated.

* In `wp_plugin_update_row()`:

  * **Security closures** (`is_security === true` or `reason === 'security-issue'`): Displays `.notice.notice-error.inline.notice-alt` with `role="alert"`: "Warning: This plugin was closed on [Date] due to a security issue and is no longer available for download. It should be uninstalled or replaced immediately."

  * **General closures:**
Displays `.notice.notice-warning.inline.notice-alt` with `role="status"`: "Notice: This plugin was closed on [Date] ([Reason]) and is no longer available for download."

  * **Outdated plugins:**
Displays `.notice.notice-warning.inline.notice-alt` with `role="status"` and the value of `outdated_notice`.

* Status badges (`Closed (Security)`, `Closed`, and `Outdated`) are rendered alongside the plugin title, with `.screen-reader-text` accessibility announcements.

=== 3. Themes Screen UI & Preview Modal

**`wp-admin/includes/theme.php`**, **`wp-admin/themes.php`**, and **`src/js/_enqueues/wp/theme.js`**

* `wp_prepare_themes_for_js()` exports `closed`, `is_suspended`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, `closedDate`, `closedReason`, and `outdatedNotice` to JavaScript.
* Theme card overlays and badges are rendered on both PHP non-JS cards and Underscore templates (`tmpl-theme` and `tmpl-theme-single`).
* Preview modals display prominent warning/error notices containing the closure date and reason.

=== 4. Site Health Check Integration

**`wp-admin/includes/class-wp-site-health.php`**

* Adds the `closed_plugins_and_themes` test under direct tests in `WP_Site_Health::get_tests()`.

* **Critical status:**

  * Triggered when an active plugin or active theme was closed due to a security issue (`is_security === true` or `reason === 'security-issue'`).
  * Includes direct deactivation/action links.

* **Recommended status:**

  * Triggered when an active plugin or theme is closed for non-security reasons or marked as outdated.

=== 5. API Client Handling

**`wp-admin/includes/plugin-install.php`** and **`wp-admin/includes/theme-install.php`**

* In `plugins_api()` and `themes_api()`:

  * Gracefully allow objects with `error => 'closed'` to pass through without converting them into a generic `WP_Error`.

* In `install_plugin_information()` and `install_theme_information()`:

  * Render a dedicated informational modal panel displaying the closure notice, date, reason, description, and slug instead of showing a fatal error screen.

----


== Testing Instructions

=== 1. Verify Unit Tests

Run the newly added PHPUnit test suites:

```bash
./vendor/bin/phpunit tests/phpunit/tests/plugins/closedPlugins.php
./vendor/bin/phpunit tests/phpunit/tests/theme/closedThemes.php
```

Both suites should pass with all assertions successful.

=== 2. Simulate Closed & Outdated Plugins

Filter `pre_http_request` or set the `update_plugins` site transient with:

* A plugin having:

  * `closed => true`
  * `is_security => true`
  * `closed_date => '2025-01-15'`
  * `closed_reason => 'security-issue'`

* A plugin having:

  * `closed => true`
  * `reason_text => 'Author Request'`
  * `closed_date => '2024-06-20'`

* A plugin having:

  * `is_outdated => true`

Visit `wp-admin/plugins.php` and verify that the corresponding badges are displayed next to the plugin names:

* Red: `Closed (Security)`
* Grey: `Closed`
* Yellow: `Outdated`

Also verify that the inline notice rows display the correct text, ARIA roles, and styling.

=== 3. Check Site Health

Activate a plugin marked with `is_security => true` and navigate to:

`wp-admin/site-health.php`

Verify that Site Health reports a **Critical** status issue advising immediate deactivation and deletion, and that a direct deactivation link with a valid nonce is provided.

=== 4. View Plugin & Theme Information Modals

Visit:

`wp-admin/plugin-install.php?tab=plugin-information&plugin=[closed-slug]&TB_iframe=true`

Confirm that a dedicated informational panel is displayed containing the closure date, reason, and description instead of the generic error message.

summary: Users with "same" email address can be accidentally created
_description:
Wordpress does not permit multiple users with the same email address, using RFC 5321 to define the localpart of the address.
However, several major email service providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo) ignore mixed case in localparts.
This means that WordPress will support 2 users with email addresses abc@gmail.com and ABc@gmail.com - although those 2 addresses represent the same mailbox.
Propose an enhancement:
  1. Warn admins when manually creating a user that the new email address might be a duplicate of...
  2. Highlight email addresses on the admin Users page that are case-insensitive identical.

summary: Remove login test cookie.
_description:
Follow up to r6009 for #2039.

The year is 2007, the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browser_wars#Second_browser_war_(2004%E2%80%932017) second browser war] is in its early days and has ten years to run; the most popular social media network is Myspace and WordPress introduces a test cookie the login screen because cookies can not be presumed to be available.

The year is 2027, browsers now work together for [https://wpt.fyi/interop-2026 Interoperability], social media is fractured, and -- significantly for this ticket -- **first party cookies can be presumed to be available**.

My proposal is to remove the test cookie from the login screen. Many CDNs are configured to bypass caching for cookies prefixed `wordpress_` or `wp_`, although the smarter ones ignore `wordpress_test_cookie`.

An alternative to removing the test cookie entirely is to provide a filter to allow for it to be enabled by developers if required. If this is the preferred option I suggest the filter be opt-in rather than opt-out.

summary: Block Hooks: Skip parsing and re-serializing post content in the_content when no blocks are hooked
_description:
Pages with a lot of block content are slow because, since 6.8, every the_content call parses and re-serializes the whole post even when no block is hooked, and the per-block Block Hooks visitors run on top of that.

[58291] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/b39f58ec3eab0f2b66dccebbf0fc97baaaaa9a15 b39f58ec]) returned early from apply_block_hooks_to_content() when nothing was hooked.
[59101] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/2952e563aae229fe497e723996cc5a58b92e1401 2952e563], #61902) removed that early return so template parts still get the theme attribute. Parsing and serializing now always run, and the has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) check only selects the visitors ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1171 blocks.php:1171]).
[60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/e800c60ec09a06cf73407f992d7ed1352e3c3973 e800c60e], #63287, in 6.8.1) added a temporary hooked_block_types filter inside apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06/src/wp-includes/blocks.php#L1354-L1356 blocks.php:1354-1356]). That filter makes the has_filter() check always true on this path, so the per-block visitors always run.
The PRs for [60173] ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8695 8695], [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/8700 8700]) do not mention this, and it appears to be unintended.

Timing apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object() on ~1 MB of block markup with nothing hooked (PHP 8.4):

trunk: 34-35 ms per call
with the patch: 0.4 ms per call
=== Steps to reproduce ===

In the PHPUnit test environment on trunk [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/0004f4d2e149e41dab07cfdf3e019f4a96cb4e06 0004f4d2], with no plugins and no hooked blocks, create a post with ~1 MB of nested paragraph, group and columns blocks.
Time repeated calls of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object( $post->post_content, $post ).
Expected: the content is not parsed when nothing is hooked. Actual: it is parsed and re-serialized on every call.
=== Proposed fix ===

Return the content unchanged at the top of apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object(), before the temporary filter is added, when:

get_hooked_blocks() is empty and has_filter( 'hooked_block_types' ) is false;
has_block( 'core/template-part', $content ) is false;
$ignored_hooked_blocks_at_root is null (REST passes an empty array, which keeps the full path, #65008).
Output is unchanged for well-formed content. Content with a stray closing delimiter renders as it did before 6.8. (Since 6.8, the temporary wrapper block has been making the parser recover and render those broken blocks anyway, and the patch removes that recovery whenever it skips the pass.)

The patch adds one test, test_apply_block_hooks_to_content_from_post_object_returns_content_unchanged_if_no_hooked_blocks, to applyBlockHooksToContentFromPostObject.php. Run with php vendor/bin/phpunit --group block-hooks (SQLite).

AI assistance: Yes
Tool(s): Claude Code, Codex CLI
Model(s): Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra
Used for: root-cause analysis, git history checks, patch, test and benchmark drafting, accuracy review; 
I reviewed the patch and the claims.

summary: Toolbar: one search entry point for the admin and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes one search entry point in the Toolbar. The front end gets the same search item the admin has, in the same place and with the same shortcut.

=== Current behavior ===

The Toolbar has two search controls. They share the same icon, but they work in different ways.

 * In the admin, the item sits on the left, after the site name. It shows the icon and the shortcut (⌘K or Ctrl+K) and it opens the command palette.
 * On the front end, the item sits on the far right, after the account item. It is a field that expands on focus and opens the site search results. It has no shortcut.

On small screens the front-end search is hidden, so the Toolbar has no search there.

The field is also the reason the account item is not the last item on the right on the front end. Which create an odd inconsistency. 

[[Image(before-front-toolbar.png)]]

=== Proposal ===

 * Remove the search field from the right side of the front-end Toolbar.
 * Show the same item the admin has, in the same position, with the same icon and shortcut.
 * On the front end, the item and the shortcut open a small dialog with one field: "Search the site". Enter opens the site search results, same as today.
 * In the admin nothing changes. The item opens the command palette. 

[[Image(after-front-toolbar.png)]]

The dialog follows the look of the command palette, so both read as the same control.

[[Image(after-front-search-dialog.png)]]

=== No React, almost no weight ===

This proposal does not bring the command palette to the front end.

The dialog is a native `<dialog>` element with a plain search form. It needs no React and no editor packages. In my prototype it adds around 4 KB for logged-in users. For comparison, loading the command palette on the front end added around 1.6 MB of scripts (uncompressed) in the same test.

The weight was the main concern when the command palette on the front end was discussed before. This approach avoids it.

=== Why ===

 * One mental model. One icon, one place and one shortcut to search, in the admin and on the site.
 * The item does not move. The Toolbar is the only part of the interface that follows the user between the site and the admin. I believe its controls should stay in the same place when the user crosses.
 * The account item becomes the last item on the right in both contexts.
 * More space on the right side, where plugins and hosts add their own items. Same goal as #66157.
 * Search comes back on small screens.
 * Nothing is lost. The search does the same thing it does today.

=== Accessibility ===

 * The same shortcut works in both contexts.
 * The dialog moves focus to the field when it opens. Escape closes it and focus returns to the Toolbar item. The browser handles this natively.
 * The field has a clear name, "Search the site". Today the label is only "Search".
 * The Toolbar keeps its layout on focus. Today the field grows inside it.
 * Without JavaScript, the item can be a plain link to the search page.
 * RTL: no change, the item mirrors as in the admin.

=== Backward compatibility ===

 * The search request is the same (`?s=`). Themes and search plugins keep working.
 * Code that removes the search item keeps working, there is nothing to remove.
 * Custom CSS for the old field stops applying.
 * "Search the site" is a new string.

=== Follow-up ===

The command palette could use the same label and offer a "Search the site for …" result. Then both contexts answer the same way. This part lives in Gutenberg, so it needs its own issue.

=== Related ===

 * #65221 has the same goal and keeps the field on the right. This ticket goes one step further.
 * #64672 added the command palette item to the Toolbar.
 * #64875 discusses the position of that item.
 * #26940 is an older proposal for the front-end search.
 * #66157 frees space on the right side.
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/73708 Gutenberg #73708] discussed the command palette on the front end.

summary: Inconsistency in date setting when changing post status
_description:
In my opinion the behaviour of WP is inconsistent regarding setting the post date when changing a post status draft to published:
– Using single post editing or Quick Edit, the former post date is being restored, while

summary: Reconcile styles of data tables (WP_List_Table, DataViews)
_description:
Currently, the WordPress admin has two different ways of displaying tables of data: PHP-based screens like the "Posts" like use [https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/classes/wp_list_table/ WP_List_Table], while React-based screens like the site editor ("Appearance" > "Editor") use [https://developer.wordpress.org/block-editor/reference-guides/packages/packages-dataviews/ DataViews].

**Problem:** As can be seen in the attached screenshots that follow, there are a number of different stylistic differences between WP_List_Table and DataViews:

- Column heading casing (sentence case in WP_List_Table, all-caps in DataViews)
- Column sort button using different icons
- Row column background (alternating white/gray in WP_List_Table, non-alternating in DataViews)
- Border styling (no borders between rows in WP_List_Table, borders in DataViews)
- Table headings placement (both at top and bottom in WP_List_Table, only at top in DataViews)
- ...and more

As part of the effort to adopt a uniform [https://wordpress.github.io/gutenberg/?path=/docs/design-system-introduction--docs design system] across the WordPress admin, these differences are problematic:

- From a user's perspective, the difference is noticeable, and they don't feel like they're part of the same product. Learning to use one style of presentation doesn't extend to the other.
- From a contributor's perspective, maintaining two different styles of tables requires duplicated styles, and it's unclear what is the singular intended appearance of tables in the admin.

**Expected outcome:** Align on a unified style for tables, working through differences like those listed above to come to a common approach, and implement it.

summary: REST API: rest_filter_response_fields() fatals on PHP 8 when response data is stdClass (e.g. /wp/v2/taxonomies?type=…&_fields=…)
_description:
On PHP 8+, requesting a taxonomy collection with _fields can fatal instead of returning a trimmed JSON response.

rest_filter_response_fields() passes response data into _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive(), which calls array_intersect_key() without ensuring the value is an array. When WP_REST_Response::get_data() is a stdClass (seen with /wp/v2/taxonomies?type={post_type}&_fields=…), PHP throws:

TypeError: array_intersect_key(): Argument #1 ($array) must be of type array, stdClass given
in wp-includes/rest-api.php (_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
Related: for slug-keyed collections such as /wp/v2/taxonomies and /wp/v2/types, _fields intersects top-level keys (taxonomy/type slugs) with field names (name, slug, …), so a successful response is often an empty array [] even when taxonomies exist. Filtering should be applied per item in the collection.

== Steps to reproduce
Site on PHP 8.0+ with at least one public custom post type that has a REST-visible taxonomy (e.g. CPT UI testimonial + testimonial_category), or any setup that yields object-shaped taxonomy collection data for a type filter.
While logged in (or with sufficient caps), open or request:
GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?type=testimonial&_fields=name,slug,rest_base,hierarchical,types
(Substitute any post type slug that has associated taxonomies.)

Observe HTTP 500 and the TypeError above in the error log.
Also compare:

`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies`
`GET /wp-json/wp/v2/taxonomies?_fields=name,slug,types,rest_base`

The second often returns [] even though the first returns a non-empty object keyed by taxonomy slug.

== Expected behavior
No fatal.
_fields returns a trimmed representation of each taxonomy in the collection.
Non-array response data is coerced to an array (or skipped) before array_intersect_key().
Actual behavior
Uncaught TypeError in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() when data is stdClass.

== Environment
WordPress 6.x / 7.x (reproduced with current rest_filter_response_fields / _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive)
PHP 8.x (strict types on array_intersect_key())
Triggered from the block editor / CPT UI (User-Agent: node) hitting the taxonomies endpoint after editing a CPT
Code pointer
wp-includes/rest-api.php:

rest_filter_response_fields()
_rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() — assumes $array1 is always an array
rest_api_default_filters() re-registers rest_filter_response_fields on rest_api_init.

== Suggested fix
Guard/coerce in _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() / rest_filter_response_fields():

{{{#!php
<?php
if ( is_object( $data ) ) {
    $data = get_object_vars( $data ); // or recursive array cast
}
if ( ! is_array( $data ) ) {
    return $response;
}
}}}

For non-numeric collections whose values are arrays/objects and whose keys are not in the _fields list, apply _rest_array_intersect_key_recursive() to each item (same idea as the wp_is_numeric_array() branch).

summary: Make the Core E2E tests preserve the development environment state
_description:
Related: #63532.

The Core E2E setup makes the test run on the development database. This is inconsistent with the PHPUnit tests which run on the tests database, when properly configured.

Also, some methods provided by the `e2e-test-utils-playwright` package, like `deleteAllMedia()` are inherently dangerous because they literally delete ''all'' attachments, including the existing ones. This is inconsistent with the PHPUnit tests setup which makes its best to preserve the contents of the uploads directory.

This issue should be reported upstream in the Gutenberg repository to be considered for the packages provided there. However, it also affects the Core E2E setup, which is existing code in Core and should be tested in Core.

To reproduce:
- Make sure your development environment does have a few posts and comments.
- Make sure it also has some uploaded attachments.
- Set some user preferences, for example go to the Media Library and click the 'Grid view' link. Your choice will be saved in the persisted user preferences.
- From the terminal, run `npm run test:e2e`.
- Once the tests complete, observe that:
  - All your posts have been deleted.
  - All the comments have been deleted.
  - All your blocks (post type = wp_block), if any, have been deleted.
  - Your preferences have been reset. E.g. the Media Library will default to the 'List' view.

The E2E tests global setup, and also some specific tests, use the following methods that are responsible for the deletions:

- `requestUtils.deleteAllPosts()`: Deletes all posts of type `post`. As such, Core deletes all the related comments as well.
- `requestUtils.deleteAllBlocks()`: Deletes all blocks (post type = wp_block).
- `requestUtils.resetPreferences()`: Resets all user persisted preferences.

Additionally, there are a few more 'dangerous' methods provided by the E@E test utils. For example: `requestUtils.deleteAllMedia()` is not currently used in the tests but it's dangerous as it literally delets all attachments, even the pre-existing ones in your development environment.

Ideally:
- The tests should run on the tests database.
- Any file operation for the attachments should use its own uploads directory, not the default 'uploads' one, as proposed for the PHPUnit tests in #63532.

summary: REST API: Attachment title from uploaded filename is not sanitized like media library uploads
_description: When a file is uploaded through the REST API (`POST /wp/v2/media`, used by the block editor) without a title, the attachment title is built from the raw uploaded filename and never sanitized. Chrome and other browsers send a double quote in a multipart filename as `%22`. So uploading `"css".png` from the block editor creates an attachment titled **`%22css%22`**. Uploading the same file through the media library (`async-upload.php` → `media_handle_upload()`) gives the title `css`, because `media_handle_upload()` runs the name through `sanitize_text_field()`. The REST logic was added in [58447] (#57957) to "match the naming behavior for uploaded media in the REST API to the way media is named when uploading in the media library", but it doesn't apply the same sanitization. HTML in a filename is kept as well: `Bold Name.jpg` gets the title `Bold Name` via REST, and `Bold Name` via the media library. === Steps to reproduce 1. In Chrome, open the block editor and add an Image block. 2. Upload a file named `"css".png`. 3. Check the attachment title in the media library: it shows `%22css%22`. === Expected The title should be `css`, the same as an upload through the media library. === Proposed fix Wrap the derived title in `sanitize_text_field()` in `WP_REST_Attachments_Controller::insert_attachment()`, as `media_handle_upload()` does. Found while testing #16191. The related ''filename'' issue (`22css22.png`) is tracked in #66125.

summary: Same-site post embeds get a doubled #?secret= fragment, breaking the resize/reveal handshake
_description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. On any post, add a core Embed block pointing at a URL on the same site (another post, page, or product).
2. View the post on the front end.
3. Inspect the resulting <iframe class="wp-embedded-content">.

Expected: src="https://example.com/target/embed/#?secret=XXXXXXXXXX"

Actual: src="https://example.com/target/embed/#?secret=XXXXXXXXXX#?secret=YYYYYYYYYY" — two #?secret= fragments concatenated.

Why it matters: wp-embed.min.js reveals and resizes the iframe only after the embedded page reports back the secret via postMessage, matched against data-secret. With a malformed double-hash, the embedded page reads back the wrong (first) secret, the check fails, and the iframe is left permanently visibility: hidden. The post looks broken — an empty gap where the embed should be — with no error anywhere.

Root cause: get_post_embed_html() (wp-includes/embed.php) builds the local embed's HTML and appends #?secret=$secret to the iframe src. That HTML then passes through wp_filter_oembed_result() (hooked on oembed_dataparse), which regexes out the existing src value and appends another #?secret=$secret on top, without first stripping the one already there.

Reproduction environment: confirmed on a clean install, default theme, zero plugins active — not theme- or plugin-specific.

Suggested fix: in wp_filter_oembed_result(), strip any existing #?secret=... from $results[2] before appending the new one, e.g. preg_replace('/#\?secret=[^#]*/', '', $results[2]).

Checked for duplicates: searched all open tickets in the Embeds component and several targeted queries (secret, wp_filter_oembed_result, data-secret) — no existing report found.

summary: Further hardening of MO file parsing
_description:
**Description**

`WP_Translation_File_MO::parse_file()` already performs some validation when parsing `.mo` files. See #61794, which added hardening for invalid metadata lines.

There are still other parts of the MO file structure that are not fully validated before being used. In particular, offsets and lengths from the MO header and translation tables are used to calculate table boundaries and read strings without consistently verifying that they describe valid ranges within the file.

Malformed or truncated MO files could therefore result in unexpected parsing behaviour.

**Expected behavior**

The MO parser should reject structurally invalid files cleanly with an `Invalid data` error, while continuing to accept valid MO files.

This would extend the existing hardening introduced in #61794 to the remaining structural data of the MO file.

summary: Ensure valid HTML when using the myblogs_options filter
_description:
Discovered while reviewing #66205 / [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13819 PR 13819] In the Network admin, in the `my-sites.php` page, there are two filters (technically it's the same filter with a different 'context'): `$settings_html = apply_filters( 'myblogs_options', '', 'global' );` and `echo apply_filters( 'myblogs_options', '', $user_blog );` They are meant to pass additional HTML to be printed on the page. 1 The first filter prints the additional HTML above the sites 'cards'. It also prints a hardcoded heading 'Global Settings'. However, the filter is placed right after a `
    ` opening tag. As such, when the filter is in use, the heading and the passed HTMl are printed out as children of the `
      ` element. That's invalid HTML. It may also make assistive technology confused when announcing the count of the items within the list. Example: {{{

        Global Settings

        {any additional passed HTML here} }}} 2 The second filter is meant to print additional HTML ''inside'' the sites 'cards'. It is placed inside a `
      • ` tag. List items can contain almost any kind of elements so valid HTML isn't a big concern in this case. However, the filter documentation doesn't mention in any way that the passed HTML will be printed out inside a list item, it only references the first filter documentation. Given the actual usage of these filters renders HTML in different ways, the documentation should make clear what kind of HTML is expected and how to ensure it is valid.

summary: KSES: Re-implement using HTML API
_description:
Since its initial commit, WordPress has relied on the KSES library to sanitize and normalize and transform content from untrusted sources. Unfortunately, the parsing inside of `wp_kses()` has never been spec-compliant, leading to numerous challenges in safely, efficiently, and reliably fulfilling its purpose.

The HTML API provides a mechanism for structurally interacting with HTML in an efficient manner, and `wp_kses()` should be rewritten to lean on that existing capability.

== Resolves

 - #25851 Large attribute values may crash PCRE patterns and cause content loss.
 - #37698 Global pollution in `wp_kses_split()` calls.
 - #48873 CSS contents are corrupted by `wp_kses()`.
 - #51482 `wp_kses()` turns SCRIPT and STYLE content into renderable text.
 - #52333 `wp_kses()` and HTML disagree on the set of named character references.
 - #58377 Block names with consecutive hyphens are corrupted.
 - #58921 Valid tag names are rejected from the allow-list.
 - #59310 `parse_blocks()` called unnecessarily.
 - #61246 `wp_kses()` un-comments HTML comments.
 - #62024 `wp_kses_post()` incorrectly escapes “<” in attribute values.

=== Potentially resolves

 - #51093 CSS `>` corruption.
 - #56118 Slashes are improperly stripped when exporting data.

== Related

 - #63881 Deprecate `wp_kses_stripslashes()`.
 - #65599 HTML sanitization API implementation.

summary: Position block support: derive container class from styles so identical rules are deduplicated
_description:
`wp_render_position_support()` builds its container class from a per-request counter:

{{{#!php
<?php
$class_name = wp_unique_id( 'wp-container-' );
}}}

Every block instance with position support therefore gets its own class and its own rule in the `block-supports` style engine store, even when the resulting CSS is byte-for-byte identical.

The other block supports that emit a scoped rule derive the class from the style inputs, so identical styles collapse into one rule:

||= Support =||= Class strategy =||
|| `layout.php` || `wp_unique_id_from_values( $hash_input, 'wp-container-' )` ||
|| `custom-css.php` || `wp_unique_id_from_values( $parsed_block, ... )` ||
|| `states.php` || `md5()` of the rules ||
|| `settings.php` || `md5( serialize( $block ) )` ||
|| **`position.php`** || **`wp_unique_id()` (counter)** ||

`wp_render_layout_support_flag()` documents why it hashes: to keep class names the same for blocks with the same definition, and stable across paginations such as the Query block's enhanced pagination. Position uses the same `wp-container-` prefix but doesn't get that behaviour.

=== Impact ===

With 200 Group blocks that all use `position: sticky; top: 0px`:

||= =||= Rules in store =||= Generated CSS =||
|| trunk || 200 || 22,092 bytes ||
|| patched || 1 || 116 bytes ||

This CSS is inlined into every front-end response, so the duplication adds page weight on every request, on top of the render cost.

Typography: Add font-stretch and font-variation-settings support to Theme JSON styles
_description:
Related: Gutenberg [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/issues/83148 83148] is the design discussion, and [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/83159 83159] is the editor prototype. This ticket is not a proposal to move that discussion here: it covers only the Core-side contract two typography style properties need, so that the editor work has somewhere to land. Which controls appear, and what a font's faces say they can do, stay in Gutenberg.

== What this adds ==

Two style properties, each stored under `styles.typography` and written by the style engine:

|| Stored as || Written as ||
|| `fontStretch` || `font-stretch` ||
|| `fontVariationSettings` || `font-variation-settings` ||

With them:

* `settings.typography.fontStretch`, alongside the existing `fontStyle` and `fontWeight`, and on by default in `wp-includes/theme.json`.
* `settings.typography.fontVariations`, a boolean saying whether a site offers editing of a font's custom axes at all.
* `axes` on a font face, so a face can say which OpenType axes it has and over what range.
* `font-variation-settings` in the list `safecss_filter_attr()` allows. `font-stretch` is already there.
* `fontStretch` and `fontVariationSettings` as typography block supports.
* Tests for the block support, the style engine and `WP_Theme_JSON`.

== Why a width needs a property of its own ==

`font-stretch` is the only axis of the four that map to a CSS property which a browser will not stand in for: there is no `font-synthesis-width` to go with `font-synthesis-weight` and `font-synthesis-style`. A variable font that declares a width range has nothing in Core today that can carry a chosen width, so the value has to be written by hand.

The name is the older one deliberately. CSS Fonts 4 renames the property `font-width` and keeps `font-stretch` as its legacy alias; no browser implements `font-width` yet, and the alias drives the `wdth` axis identically.

== Why the variation settings value is an object ==

`font-variation-settings` replaces the whole list rather than merging, so a string value cannot be inherited through the theme.json origins the way other styles are: setting one axis on a block would mean repeating every axis the root set. Keyed by tag, origins merge per axis, and the style engine assembles the string once at the boundary.

The four axes that have a property of their own — `wght`, `wdth`, `slnt`, `ital` — are refused there. The property is applied after the properties that map to the same axis, so a coordinate written here takes the axis away from the control that owns it: `font-weight: 700` with `"wght" 400` renders at 400, and a `<strong>` inside an element carrying `"wght" 300` does not get bolder. `opsz` is allowed, because `font-optical-sizing` can only switch the browser's own tracking on or off and has no way to carry a chosen size.

A tag must be four letters or digits, which is what OpenType allows and also keeps quotation marks out of the serialized value, and a value must be a number rather than a numeric string. Those rules live in one place, `WP_Style_Engine`, and `WP_Theme_JSON` reads them through it when it sanitizes rather than repeating them.

== What is not here ==

* The editor controls, and the reading of a family's faces that decides what they offer. That is Gutenberg's, and #83148 has the model.
* Which blocks opt in. The supports exist; no block in this patch turns them on.
* Reading `axes` from a font file's `fvar` table on upload. The contract is here so that a theme can declare it; the Font Library reading it is separate work.

summary: wpmu_activate_signup() reports a password that was never set when the user already exists
_description:
In `wpmu_activate_signup()`, `$password` is generated before the `username_exists()` check. If the user already exists and the signup includes a site, that password is never applied to the account, but it is still:

 * passed to the `wpmu_activate_blog` action,
 * emailed by `wpmu_welcome_notification()` through the default `Password: PASSWORD` template,
 * displayed on `wp-activate.php`.

[49078] documented `$password` as "User password, or "N/A" if the user account is not new" for `wpmu_welcome_notification()`, and `wp-admin/network/site-new.php` already passes `'N/A'`, but `wpmu_activate_signup()` never does.

=== Steps to reproduce ===

 1. On a multisite with site registration enabled, create a site signup for a new user via `wp-signup.php`.
 2. Make the first activation fail during site creation, for example by adding an error on `wp_validate_site_data`. The user is created, the site is not.
 3. Visit the activation link again.

**Expected:** the page and welcome email do not show a password, since none was generated for the account.
**Actual:** the site is created, and the page and welcome email show a new password that does not work. The password set on the first attempt was never shown to anyone, so the user can only get in via password reset.

=== Reachability ===

Not reachable through `wp-signup.php` validation alone, since `wpmu_validate_user_signup()` rejects existing usernames. It is reachable when site creation fails partway and the link is retried, with concurrent activations of the same key, and when plugins call `wpmu_signup_blog()` for existing users.

=== Proposed fix ===

Generate the password only when the user is created in `wpmu_activate_signup()`, otherwise use `'N/A'`, matching the docblock and `site-new.php`. Patch and unit tests to follow.

Related: #38474 (PR 8710 also modifies `wpmu_activate_signup()` and adds a test class named `Tests_Multisite_wpmuActivateSignup`), #33209, #31127.

After uploading a plugin zip, link to the Plugin settings instead of the "Plugin Installer"
_description:
After a plugin is installed by uploading a zip (Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin), the result screen shows "Activate Plugin", and once that's done a "Go to Plugin Installer" link pointing to `plugin-install.php`.

Nobody who just uploaded a plugin needs the Plugin Installer next :)

They uploaded a zip, so they weren't browsing the directory. The useful place to go is the Plugin's settings page (?). 

"Go to Plugin Installer" is the only way off the screen, and it goes to the wrong place.

=== History

Before [37221] (#35429, 4.6), uploads fell through to the default "Return to Plugins page" link. That changeset moved the upload form from its own page onto the Add Plugins screen and added a dedicated `'upload' === $this->type && 'plugins' === $from` branch pointing back to the installer. That branch seems to exist only to send users back to where the form now lives. Now that the upload form is a toggle on the installer screen, going back there has no purpose.

=== Proposed fix

Remove that branch from `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` so uploads use the existing `else` branch, "Go to Plugins page" (`plugins.php`).

Installs from the directory (`'web'`) keep "Go to Plugin Installer", since people often install several plugins in a row there. The importer flow is unchanged. There are no new strings, and sites can still change the link through the `install_plugin_complete_actions` filter.

Patch attached.

=== Testing instructions

 1. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and upload any valid plugin zip.
 2. On the result screen, confirm the secondary link reads "Go to Plugins page" and opens `plugins.php`.
 3. Install a plugin from the directory with JS disabled (`update.php?action=install-plugin`) and confirm it still shows "Go to Plugin Installer".

=== Related

 - #35429: moved the upload form onto the Add Plugins screen and introduced the installer link for uploads.
 - #60578: added the installer link to the upload error screen, a different case where the link makes sense.
 - #66184: same result screen, Activate button with unmet plugin dependencies.
 - #40651: finding plugin settings after activation, which would be the natural next step beyond this fix.

summary: After uploading a plugin that "requires" other plugins, the "Activate Plugin" button leads to a wp_die() WSOD
_description:
When a plugin is installed by uploading a zip, the result screen always shows an "Activate Plugin" button, even when the plugin's `Requires Plugins` header lists plugins that are not installed or not active. Clicking it takes the user to a bare `wp_die()` white screen with no admin menu and no way forward other than the browser's back button or the "Manage plugins" link.

[[Image()]]

The Plugins list table and the AJAX install flow already block activation in this case (the AJAX flow since #61294). The installer screen should behave the same way.

== Steps to reproduce

1. Create a plugin with this header and zip it:

{{{
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Dep Test Plugin
 * Requires Plugins: classic-editor
 */
}}}

2. Make sure the required plugin (Classic Editor in this example) is not installed on the site
3. Go to Plugins > Add New Plugin > Upload Plugin and install the zip.
4. On the result screen, click "Activate Plugin".

**Actual result:** a `wp_die()` white screen reading "Error: Dep Test Plugin requires 1 plugin to be installed and activated: Classic Editor. Manage plugins."

**Expected result:** the result screen does not offer "Activate Plugin" (or "Network Activate" on multisite) and tells the user which plugins are missing, inside the normal admin screen.

== Cause

Uploads and non-JS installs run through `update.php?action=upload-plugin` and `update.php?action=install-plugin`, which render `Plugin_Installer_Skin`. `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()` builds the activate links based only on the install result, the `activate_plugin` capability and whether the plugin is already active. It never checks the plugin's requirements, and `update.php` never initializes `WP_Plugin_Dependencies`.

The link goes to `plugins.php?action=activate`, where `activate_plugin()` calls `validate_plugin_requirements()`, gets a `plugin_missing_dependencies` error, and `plugins.php` passes it to `wp_die()`.

== Proposed fix

In `Plugin_Installer_Skin::after()`, when the install succeeded and the user can activate the plugin, call `validate_plugin_requirements()`, the same check `activate_plugin()` runs. If it returns a `WP_Error`, remove the activate and network activate links and show the error message as an admin notice.

`validate_plugin_requirements()` already calls `WP_Plugin_Dependencies::initialize()`, and `Plugin_Upgrader::install()` has already cleared the plugins cache, so the newly installed plugin's header is read correctly. Reusing this function also means the installer screen never offers a link that `activate_plugin()` would reject, including the WordPress and PHP version checks and the `validate_plugin_requirements` filter.

Patch attached.

== Testing instructions

1. Apply the patch.
2. Repeat the steps to reproduce above.
3. Confirm the result screen shows an error notice naming the missing plugin and no "Activate Plugin" button.
4. Upload a plugin without a `Requires Plugins` header and confirm "Activate Plugin" still appears.
5. Optional: repeat on multisite from Network Admin and confirm "Network Activate" is hidden only in the unmet-dependency case.

== Related

* #61294: the same bug in the AJAX install flow, fixed in 6.5.4 by adding a missed `initialize()` call.
* #64493: improving plugin dependency messages (7.2).
* #22316: the original Plugin Dependencies feature, shipped in 6.5.

summary: Add grunt ticket:<n> to read a Trac ticket, and restore grunt patch:<n>, by fetching through the Playwright browser core already ships
_description:
core.trac.wordpress.org now answers every non-browser request with a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge (`Checking your browser...`, HTTP 403). That includes the plain HTML, `?format=rss`, `?format=csv`, the attachment listing, and raw attachments. Two consequences for contributors and committers:

 1. `grunt patch:<ticket>` fails for every ticket. Reproduced today against #66079: {{{Running "patch:66079" (patch) task >> getPatchFromTicket fail >> status: 403}}}. This is tracked upstream as [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/210 grunt-patch-wordpress#210] (August 2026), with no fix.
 2. There is no way to read a ticket from the command line at all. Anyone scripting a triage or commit workflow, including AI-assisted ones, has to paste ticket text by hand.

The durable fix is a structured read API, proposed in [https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8202 meta:#8202]. That ticket is currently unowned (owner removed June 2026) and the discussion there favours either Systems restoring access for identified clients or a Trac-native MCP plugin. Neither is on a timeline.

== Proposal ==

core already ships a real browser: `@playwright/test` 1.61.1 is a devDependency, and the end-to-end and performance workflows install Chromium with `npm exec --no -- playwright install chromium`. The challenge is designed to let browsers through, so a headless Chromium page passes it in a few seconds and can then read the rendered ticket, the attachment list, and raw attachments.

Two tasks, both implemented in the `grunt-patch-wordpress` package that core already depends on, then picked up here with a dependency bump:

 * `grunt ticket:<n>` (new): prints the ticket summary, properties, description, attachments with raw URLs, linked pull requests, and the full change history. `--json` for structured output.
 * `grunt patch:<n>` (existing): swap the two `request()` calls in `getPatchFromTicket()` and `getPatch()` for fetches made through the same Playwright page, so the attachment listing and download work again. Also make the failure message say "Trac returned a bot-protection challenge" instead of "Nothing to patch", as issue 210 asks.

Prerequisite for both: `npx playwright install chromium` once, the same step the e2e suite needs. If no browser is installed the task should say exactly that and exit, not fall through to the old usage help.

A working proof of concept for the read half is at [https://github.com/whyisjake/trac-ticket whyisjake/trac-ticket]. It reads core and meta tickets, keeps the challenge cookie across runs, and takes about 6 seconds per ticket.

== Caveats worth deciding up front ==

 * This routes tooling through a protection Systems put in place. It is the project's own tool on the project's own Trac, using the exact path the challenge is meant to allow, but Systems should be looped in so they are not surprised by headless-browser traffic from committers. An allowlisted client would make all of this unnecessary.
 * It is a stopgap. When meta:#8202 or an equivalent API lands, both tasks should switch to it and drop the browser dependency.
 * Downloading Chromium is roughly 95 MB. That is already true for contributors running e2e tests; it becomes true for anyone who wants `grunt patch` back.

== Related ==

 * [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/210 grunt-patch-wordpress#210] – grunt patch fails for every ticket
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/grunt-patch-wordpress/issues/83 grunt-patch-wordpress#83] – list PRs along with patches (the new task covers this)
 * meta:#8202 – structured JSON API for Trac

AI assistance: Yes. Tool(s): Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.1). Used for: confirming the 403 behaviour and the grunt patch failure, locating the upstream issue and meta ticket, building the proof-of-concept script, and drafting this ticket.
